utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. Madam Registrar, may I ask you to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is case number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Joanna Korner, Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, and Lise-Lotte Karlsson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, and for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Any special administrative matters to be discussed before we start? I can see none. May I then ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kuruzovic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have a transcript here, and could you please answer in a way that it's reflected in the transcript. I understand by your nodding that you said yes. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is, yes. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before I ask you to give the solemn declaration, would you please be seated because I have to give you some information beforehand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, you recall that you have nearly one year ago, the 21st of March, 2002, been interviewed or interrogated by representatives of the Office of the Prosecution? At that time you learned that from the side of the Prosecution you are regarded as a suspect, a suspect but not indicted. We learned that since then nothing has changed in your role. Our Rules of Procedure and Evidence don't have any specific regulations on the rights of a suspect during trial in a case against another person, in this case the case Prosecutor versus Dr. Stakic. No doubt, however, that a fortiori, even more so Rule 42 has to be applied in analogy also during this hearing. Therefore, I have to read out the following: Rule 42 - and that's the same that was read out to you about one year ago - that reads: "That a suspect has the right to be assisted by counsel of the suspect's choice or to be assigned legal assistance without payment if the suspect does not have sufficient means to pay for it." (ii) "The right to have the assistance of a free interpreter if the suspect cannot understand or speak the language to be used for questioning." Here you can see already we have the assistance of an interpreter. You can listen to the proceedings in a language you understand. (iii) "There's the right to remain silent." And I have to caution you that any statement you would make will be recorded and maybe used in evidence even against you. This means in concreto that there is an absolute right to remain silent or you may refuse to answer any questions the reply to which would subject you to the risk of being prosecuted for a criminal offence either here in this Tribunal or elsewhere. Furthermore, Rule 42 provides that the questioning of a suspect shall not proceed without the presence of counsel unless the suspect has voluntarily waived the right to counsel. In case of waiver, if you subsequently would express a desire to have counsel, questioning shall thereupon cease and shall only resume when you have obtained or have been assigned counsel. This was a long information. Did you understand this information, or do you have any questions on these issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So may I ask you: Are you prepared to proceed without the presence of counsel and do you specifically waive your right to counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wasn't really aware that I had come here in that capacity, but I'm quite ready to continue the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And I have to repeat: In case you believe that you should change your opinion, please tell us immediately because then under Rule 42(B), second sentence, if you would express your desire to have counsel, the questioning should thereupon cease immediately and only resume when counsel would arrive. So may I then ask the usher to take the solemn declaration, Mr. Kuruzovic. Mr. Kuruzovic, would you please be so kind and stand up and give us your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The first part of questioning is dedicated to your personal data only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you please give us for the transcript your name, forename, and nickname.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Kuruzovic. I have no nicknames.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The date and place of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: 20th of February, 1942, Arandjelovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you tell us in which part of your home country Arandjelovac is situated?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: It's in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Your actual residence, please, the concrete address.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: In Prijedor, the 4th of July Street, 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what about your marital status? Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I'm married and have a son. My wife, my son, my daughter-in-law, and two granddaughters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you have another child?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had a daughter. She died in 1992. It was an aneurism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you want to give us some details? It's up to you. And it's of course your own decision -- of the death of your daughter, about the death of your daughter, the special circumstances and when exactly it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: She was in Sarajevo with her boyfriend who was studying in Sarajevo at the time, and in the evening she fell in the bathtub because she fainted. She was taken to the hospital, and they established that she had a brain haemorrhage. It is a natural anomaly, that is, the widening of the artery which carries blood to the brain. She spent a month in a Sarajevo hospital, and I was with my family there, and my wife was there and we visited her all the time. After the first surgery, it was established that the case was very complicated because it was very difficult to drain the brain of the blood, so that after a month she underwent another operation, but my daughter never woke up after the coma, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please tell us when exactly it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd of March. The 3rd of March, 1992. I was there staying with my wife's relatives because she is a Sarajevan, so that I was staying with her mother and her sister, and we were all together there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for giving us these details. Could you then, please, in context tell us briefly your education and your professional career until, say, 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from mathematics and physics. I worked in Mladen Stojanovic's school in 1981 teaching mathematics and physics. In 1981 I was appointed the principal of a school out of town, and I spent three years there as a principal. After that, I was appointed the principal of the 16th of May School in the centre of town, and I continued there until the 5th of May, 1994. After that, I spent four years as the director of Radio Prijedor and Kozarski Vjesnik. And as of 1998, I've been working in the school in which I was a principal prior to 1994, and I am now assistant principal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let us concentrate on the period following the census 1990 -- or better, 1991, of course, the election in 1990 and census 1991. In that census, what did you indicate as your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb by origin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you: Did you accept the outcome of this census or did you believe this was an illegal, illegitimate census?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, seeing that it was organised by the authorities, it was lawful and legitimate. In the papers, there were comments that the elections were not really conducted properly, and the same went for the census, that is, that there were more people in the town of other origins than it was realistic. But that was irrelevant. I respect things that are organised by official bodies. Could the microphones please be brought closer to the witness

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And for the first --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphones please be brought closer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When was it that you for the first time engaged in politics?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: One could say in -- that it was in 1960, when I became a member of the League of Communists, as the majority of young people in that country at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But then, what about - and let's focus the following questions and answers on the period starting with January 1992. Please try to tell us in a context to the best of your recollection what happened, where did you participate in the events in January -- starting January 1992 and then resulting in this heinous crimes that are part of our hearing. We have to find out the -- whether or not there is an individual responsibility of Dr. Stakic, but we have called you to come to The Hague in order to come closer to the truth and to find out what actually happened since January 1992 in Prijedor in preparation of the Serbian Municipal Assembly, in preparation of the Crisis Staff and so on. I have to give you the possibility to discuss this in context, and please the floor is yours now and we are listening to all that what you have to tell us about the events from January 1992 through, say, October 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the Orthodox Christmas, that is, the 7th of January, 1992, the Serb people formed the Assembly of the municipality, a Serb one, and at that Assembly the president of the Assembly, vice-president of the Assembly, members of the executive board were elected by voting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Whenever you mention titles, president, vice-president, could you please be so kind and at the same time add the names of these persons. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Milomir Stakic was elected the president of the Assembly; Dragan Savanovic was elected the vice-president; late Dr. Mico Kovacevic was elected the president of the executive board; the vice-president of the executive board, Bosko Mandic, was elected to that post; Slobodan Kuruzovic was elected the commander of the Territorial Defence; late Simo Drljaca was elected the head of the police, or rather, the Chief of the Public Security Station; the Secretary for Economy and Service Industries - I believe that is what it was called - Mr. Ranko Travar was elected to that post; and the secretary for general administrative affairs became now -- what's his name? If I may look up his name. Oh, yes, here it is. Svetozar Petrovic. And the head for the People's Defence, for the All People's Defence was Mr. Slavko Budimir. So those elections were carried out and these people didn't do anything in particular until the 29th, or rather, the 30th of April, except that Mr. Stakic was the vice-president of the municipality at the time, so he went to work, he worked there. I mean, that would be about it as regards that period of time. On the eve of the 29th of November -- no, before that. I think it was the 28th when dispatch arrived in the town from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I believe that the man's name was Jerko Doko he was a minister and he was issuing the order and deciding on how the prisoners should be exchanged between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and some other side which shows that there was a war in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. There was one in Slavonia. I suppose you know there were brigades which had been formed there. And also in the municipality of Prijedor to go to the front up there, that a number of people had got killed by the time, but I guess you already know that. Before that, sometime in early April power was taken over in, that is, Sanski Most, and on the 29th of April, 1992 - but I wouldn't know exactly whether it was in the morning or the afternoon - another dispatch came from the Ministry of Defence with the instruction to take over the Zarko Zgonjanin's barracks in Prijedor, to disarm the army, and I think there was some order to do with the Secretariat of the Interior, but I'm not quite sure whether it applied to all or only. So but before that, the Council for National Defence, dating back to 1991 -- July or August 1991 -- had ordered the mobilisation of the whole Territorial Defence across the municipality so that all the Territorial Defence units, that is, the reserve force, were called up and issued arms in all the neighbourhood communities, so that on that 29th, because of that order, Dr. Stakic invited those people that I listed before to the Zarko Zgonjanin's Barracks, to its commander's office, Commander Arsic's office. I think that Dr. Kovacevic came, Simo Drljaca too, Dule Jankovic. I think that this -- what's his name? Javoric was also there. But I wasn't quite sure. Cadjo and Simo Miskovic and I also arrived and we learned that that dispatch had order to disarm the troops in the barracks and assumed control over the barracks and the SUP. After the discussion, it was decided that after the night fell the power should be taken over. I suppose you already know that the chief reason, the main reason for it was that there were very many difficulties involved in the early implementation of the results of the elections. It was impossible to set up the government in the municipality and it hardly functioned until that particular date. From the papers, we knew that there were some ongoing negotiations and talks, interparty communications, but I think that one of the leaders, Mirzo Mujadzic was obstructing those negotiations so that the government was never put in place and the result of it was that there were many problems involving the enforcement of laws, the permits issued to people to build on various lots, the opening of new shops, and so on and so forth. There were also settlings of accounts between various people, nothing to do with the ethnic composition. Simply, there were many burglaries and robberies in shops and stores and places. Well, there was a lot of disarray, I could say, so that this dispatch which came from the ministry with regard to the barracks only added fuel to the fire and it was decided to put an end to this state of affairs. There was -- an agreement was reached to do that. Simo Drljaca, with the Dule Jankovic undertook to organise the takeover during the night by using the services of the reserve police. And as far as I know, Simo Drljaca, Dule Jankovic and Marko Dzenadija, did that in Cirkin Polje, and sometime around 4.00 in the morning they went to certain places - I can't remember exactly where, but I think they went to the municipal hall, to the police station, to the court -- when I say "SUP," I mean to the police station -- to the court building, and some other institutions such as the post office, the public auditing service, and so on and so forth. So those police went there, they took over the security and control in all those places, and as far as I know it was all over in about 25 minutes. Not a single bullet was fired. Nothing happened. There were no incidents or anything. I think that that was that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt at this point in time. Could you please go in some more details on what happened in Cirkin Polje, especially who was present and who gave the orders or advice, everything you recall from this event in Cirkin Polje. Could you please tell us also this in context.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you're asking about the orders as to how that was to be carried out by the police. The entire operation was under the command of Simo Drljaca, Dule Jankovic, and Marko Dzenadija. That lasted until about 5.00, and then the people who were elected at the assembly arrived in Cirkin Polje and then at 6.00 in the morning or perhaps a little before 6.00 they were taken by mini-bus to the centre of the town. They assumed that post, as one might say. So the president of the municipality, the vice-president, and the president of the executive committee and the chief of the SUP did this, and all those who were employed in those institutions regardless of their nationality were at their posts. Only these people mentioned were replaced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did this meeting start and who participated in the meeting in Cirkin Polje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: There wasn't a meeting of any kind in Cirkin Polje. It was just a matter of organisation. Simo Drljaca organised at that meeting, at that discussion in the barracks, the takeover of power. There was no meeting of any other kind there. In the course of the night, they called the reserve police. The reserve police arrived in Cirkin Polje and from Cirkin Polje went to these places that I mentioned a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You yourself had been present at Cirkin Polje at that night; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. That was in a particular building. From that point in time the staff of the Territorial Defence started functioning up until then, from 7th of January, it hadn't done anything, it didn't have any particular function. And together with the people I mentioned, I was sitting there. A mini-bus came for them and took them to the town. And then after that -- as I was the commander of the staff - that in fact wasn't a real military staff; I didn't have any soldiers or officers around me - I was alone. There was some specific tasks. The first task was when the reserve police was called and the Territorial Defence, from 1991 there were checkpoints at which checks were carried out, vehicles, people, goods passing through were checked in order to maintain peace and order, and this staff organised the supply of food, taking food to the police and to the soldiers at those checkpoints. That was one of the tasks. Another task was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt once more. Let us go step by step and day by day, especially now the meeting at Cirkin Polje. You mentioned a few persons being there. You mentioned that Simo Drljaca was the one organising that meeting. Who else was present? For example, Mr. Budimir, Mr. Travar, Dr. Stakic, Mr. Savanovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: You haven't understood me -- I apologise. There were two houses. One was the hall in Cirkin Polje, and 50 metres before that there was the building of a Slovenian company. I can't remember the name. And as we had agreed in the barracks, this Territorial Defence staff, this Serbian Territorial Defence staff was supposed to be formed there. And in the course of the night that staff was supposed to be formed. It was to include myself and two or three other members of the Territorial Defence, armed civilians, and I think that there were two or three women. Dr. Stakic came to that building where I was, Savanovic, Budimir as well, Dr. Kovacevic, Travar, and so on, Svetozar Petrovic, and they were waiting there. And when power was taken over, then I think before 6.00 in the morning they were taken to their posts. And as I said, all the other people who were working in the municipality, in the court, and in the SUP, they all remained at their posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who was the one who announced that that what was planned since the 7th of April be now implemented, based on your previous meeting you had in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. The date, the 7th of April, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, 7th of January. Of course.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 7th of January, the Serbian Municipal Assembly was formed, and in the barracks -- on the basis of Dr. Stakic's invitation, all these people came, and there was a discussion, an agreement was reached according to which a takeover of power should be carried out in order to prevent all the incidents, all the things I mentioned in the town. And the order from the Ministry of Defence was to take over the barracks and to disarm the troops, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then later on in Cirkin Polje who announced to the other persons being not present in the meeting in the barracks on Dr. Stakic's invitation, who announced to the others that the point has come now to take over power in Prijedor? Who informed them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who either. If you're referring to when power was taken over, I think that was done via the radio. But the others that I mentioned weren't here. They were there together between 4.00 and 6.00 in the morning. Dr. Stakic informed the others that in the course of the night power would be taken over, that -- I assume that this had been discussed before and that the vice-president and the president of the executive board were aware of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And when this decision was taken, what should happen with those persons being an office? For example, the at that time president of the municipal assembly, should he be informed that he shouldn't arrive the next day in his office? Should he be prohibited from coming to the office, or what should happen in this case in concreto with Professor Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, nothing in particular was agreed on. When power was taken over, there were the controls of the police forces in front of the municipality and the court and the SUP and the post office as well, and as far as I can remember on the base of what I was told the president of the municipality and the vice-president, they came to work. Before that the Serbian flag had been displayed in front of the municipality building, and they were told that power had been taken over and that as president and vice-president of the municipality and of the executive committee there were new people. They returned home, and all the others remained at their posts, and all the institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I tried to understand this development. So in the morning these persons replacing the other persons in their offices would arrive at about - and this we learned also from others - about 5.00, 6.00, before the other staff members arrived. But what now -- for example, Professor Cehajic tried to enter the building of the municipal assembly. What was planned during the meeting in the barracks, how to hinder Professor Cehajic to stay in office as elected?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, nothing in particular had been planned. The police was at the entrance and quite simply Professor Cehajic and other officials weren't allowed to enter the building and they returned home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And this was true for all the others being replaced that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we continue, may I ask you the question: You mentioned on page 8 of today's transcript that on the 7th of January there was an initiative taken for having a Serbian Assembly. This was an initiative of authorities or persons living in Prijedor, or was it based on an order from higher places?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a Serbian Assembly was formed, or rather, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this is not the only municipality where Serbian assemblies were elected and formed. I'm not sure of this, but I assume that it was done via SDS parties or perhaps other organs. I assume that this was also done in Prijedor and that the Serbian Assembly of the Municipality of Prijedor was formed on the 7th of January. There was the Autonomous Region of Krajina, there was the SAO Krajina. These were all Serbian forms of organising the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And just as a follow-up: Who in fact was the person inviting and what were the criteria for inviting the others meeting at this date, the 7th of January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that it went through the Serbian Democratic Party and other Serbian parties, the Radical Party, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I know this is no more than ten years ago, so it's maybe difficult to recall. But I think it's a very -- it was a very impressive situation for you being invited for such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's not reflected on the transcript. You said "da." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That meeting, it was the assembly session. It was held in a theatre, in a big hall that has 300 seats, a capacity of 300, and all the organs of the Serbian Democratic Party delegated people in municipalities, in local communes who would be attending, who would attend the assembly, and then the organs, or rather, people would be elected. And as far as I know, nothing functioned until the 29th of April, 1992. It only existed in theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you recall who it was who invited you to attend this meeting, the 7th of April -- the 7th of January, sorry once again?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, it was up in -- it was held up in Urije. There was a local committee of the Serbian Democratic Party. The people met. That part of the organisation of the Serbian Democratic Party met there, and they delegated members of the assembly. I wasn't there on my own from that part of the town. There were other people there, I can't remember who exactly. And that's what took place in all the parts of the towns in the local communes, in the neighbourhoods. People were delegated who were to attend that session of the assembly. Then there were elections, and the assembly was formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But once again, did you get an invitation in writing or an oral invitation and then by whom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, really, as far as the assembly is concerned, I can't remember. I know that I was elected as a representative of the assembly and the local commune, and we were informed when the assembly session would be held. I can't remember whether this was done orally or whether it was in written form and then it was an invitation for the 7th of January and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Which had this session, the 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I think some working Presidency was elected. But it's a day that I can't really remember. I think at the time the president of the party in Prijedor was Simo Miskovic and the vice-president was Dragan Savanovic. I think there was some sort of chair which organised the work of the assembly. Elections were held, ballots were distributed, democratic elections were held, and the assembly was formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Why was it that a non-member of the SDS was elected president for this Serbian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if that has to do with Dr. Milomir Stakic, I don't know whether he was or wasn't. I think he was but I really don't know because I wasn't in a position to check whether he was an SDS member or not. I don't think that someone who wasn't a member of the SDS would have become the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So to the best of your recollection, the conclusion would be correct that the question of the membership in the party of the SDS was not discussed publicly during this meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: During this meeting, were there given any speeches by other persons, be it from Banja Luka or higher representatives of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember. I assume that. Perhaps the president of the municipal assembly gave a speech, Miskovic, but I don't remember exactly. I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to have an impression on what really happened, were persons -- just to give you a few names, persons like Mr. Karadzic, Ms. Plavsic, or Mr. Krajisnik, were they present during this meeting as representatives from a higher level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so, not on a single occasion. I don't remember exactly, but I don't think they were ever there on a single occasion. These names are too important for me to forget, unless my memory fails me. I'm 61. Perhaps I'm too old. So maybe I've forgotten, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's go one step further. Was there any meeting in between 7th of January and then you mentioned the 29th of April, isn't it true that there was a meeting sometime mid-April when some persons were elected, for example, Mr. Budimir and Mr. Travar and others? Do you recall this meeting in the utilities factory, I think it was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember. If there was such a meeting, I probably didn't attend it. I don't know. Between the 7th of January and the 29th of April, attended by Budimir and Travar? I assume you want to say that some sort of decisions were taken or something like that, but I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's concentrate now on the development following the takeover as of the 30th of April. Could you please tell us in some detail what especially was your work when you started this day.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you about that, because I continued as the school principal at the same time, so that it wasn't the conventional military staff. There were very few men there. There was I as a commander and two or three men who were the security and a few women, and we had taken on an auxiliary building for our use but there were no facilities to prepare food there, so that we brought our food from a canteen and our bread from Zitopromet. However, later on we started preparing our meals there and then distributing it to the checkpoints where they were together -- I mean, the Territorial Defence, or rather, military and civilians, that is, policemen. So that was the chief task of that staff, one of its main duties, and that was done at the urging, that is, I and everybody else. It was the executive board -- the executive board which urged us to move out of the municipal hall and to undertake to issue -- I mean, the Territorial Defence staff to issue vouchers, to issue fuel, petrol vouchers, petrol coupons there, so that companies and self-employed entrepreneurs and physical persons, those who needed fuels had to go there to be issued with some kind of vouchers so they could get fuel. It was simply for reasons of austerity because there were not enough oil derivatives, that is, petrol, so that we tried to avoid any excesses and we avoided giving people vouchers for larger quantities. But meanwhile, with other members of the executive board, talked with many people in neighbourhood communities, with Muslims and people in the SDA and Croats in the HDZ, inviting them to help, to maintain peace and order because all the way up to the 29th or the 30th of May there was law and order in the town in the true sense of the word. And I also participated in these discussions in the neighbourhood community in the area with the majority Muslim population. That was helped by Dedo Crnalic and Dr. Sadikovic, so we talked there and decided that it would be advisable to keep the weapons there, because in the neighbourhood community, that was the Territorial Defence to -- some hodza, I don't remember what his name was, had taken it and they panicked because there was some slight shootings, but then it was agreed and I also talked with Kapetanovic from Puharska that I and other people, that there also should be maintained order because there was also the premises of the neighbourhood community and there were troops there, but we managed to reach an understanding and there were problems and then we talked with Imam, with hodza from Cela. I believe his name was Solo, and he also helped to prevent any problems in Cela, that is, to maintain peace and order there so that -- and we also talked with representatives of the party regarding the organisation of life in Kozarac, because there were some difficulties there. The police there wouldn't put on the insignia of one ethnicity, that is, the insignia of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I think discussions there failed, the talks there failed because we were resisting, that the weapons that people had in Kozarac, because it was quite populous, so we thought that this -- these weapons and the Territorial Defence should put all these weapons in one place and to have the police guard it. We wanted to take it up there, but they refused to do that, and that was that as far as I know. So that went on until -- I'm talking about the law and order and respect for law and all that. It lasted until about the end -- the latter half of May, on the 22nd of May a military patrol was attacked while on its way to Hambarine. Namely, in all those neighbourhood communities, Hambarine and others - I won't go into them - where there were some checkpoints of the Territorial Defence, and it was formed depending on the structure of the population in those neighbourhood communities, and they were the ones who were controlling the traffic, either in the direction of Kozarac or Hambarine or Tukovi or other places. It was all -- that is, one could go through, but one had to pass through the control and one -- and no weapons were allowed. And then a patrol came up but fire was opened on them. I've forgotten whether his name was Aziz Saliskovic or whatever. I think there were six of them, and two were killed. And that is how problems started. And over there in Kozarac the Territorial Defence had set up a checkpoint, and I think they stopped the traffic there completely. One had to take a round-about road to get to the town. And there there was an attack too. I don't remember exactly how many people were involved or how many people died, but I think that the military command had issued an ultimatum to remove it. Now, I don't remember whether it was 24 hours or 48 hours. I think it was not done, and then the army went there to remove that checkpoint and that is how problems started there. In Kozarac there was gunfire, there were losses amongst the army troops and the other side, and that's how it went on. Then - and I don't remember whether it was on the 18th or the 19th of May - when I asked Commander Arsic to allow me to take a group of people to Nova Varos which is across the Sava as you pass Gradiska in the direction of Okucani. I mean I knew that combat operations had been taking place there since the autumn of 1991 and I therefore asked and took, this Dedo Crnalic, Dr. Sadikovic, Rizo Beglerbegovic, who was a big director of Markovic. Ostoja Marjanovic who was the director of the iron ore mine, and there were two -- no, through Sadikovic I also managed to get to people in Carakovo to invite them. Three guys, I think they were, with a camera, to record it. There were also two or three from Kozarac, Blagoje Gajic, the president of the war veterans unit, and so on. I don't remember how many people, but we used a minivan and I took them over there and going come coming back didn't last longer than two or three hours. That is, I took them there to show them what it looks like when there is combat, that there were houses that had been burnt down, houses that had been destroyed, that it was gone, that all the livestock was gone, that people were gone. I took them there to show it. We were allowed to cross over and allowed us to come back. And when we came back, I begged them, I asked them to talk to people, to try to show people that all this would serve no good end whatsoever. There were people from Carakovo, Hambarine and other places who were with them because I wanted us all to help to prevent, to forestall a conflict. But you know what outcome of that all. That is why I'm here today. So that's as far as that goes. The staff was then disbanded on the 16th or the 17th of May. The order came from Colonel Arsic to attach -- to resubordinate the command. Now, I don't remember whether it was the 43rd or the 343rd, but it also applied to the Territorial Defence staff. I mean, the official one, which existed there and which was under the command of Rade Javoric. That one was never disbanded, but this shows as a matter of fact all these Territorial Defence units in the town and across the municipality were under the command of that staff, and these other staff existed more or less only formally and helped with food and supplies and things like that. So that on the 17th it ceased to exist officially and -- and it was an order or a decision, whether it was the 29th or the 30th, when the official staff of the municipality was also disbanded. And so that my office also ended there. I mean, as the commander of that staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind and then continue telling us what happened from your own perspective in the following days.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in the Prijedor municipality? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these operations started -- I mean, there was an attack launched on the town. A large group of people crossed the Sana from Hambarine -- or rather, Brdo, as we call it, and with weapons attacked all the checkpoints round the bridge, La Pont, which is a fisherman's society around the church, towards Tenis [phoen], as said, along a very broad front they breached the town and reached the municipal hall, and I can't remember exactly but I think that 16 men died -- I mean, 16 Serbs. Well, perhaps it is not for me to say, but when the power was taken over from the 29th and the 30th not a bullet was fired, nobody was hurt. Now, when they tried, when they made this incursion into the town, lots of people died. There were many losses. And at about the same time problems arose over there. I mean, the fighting in Kozarac. And as far as I know, the army returned the fire, and I think that in Stari Grad towards Hambarine some tanks were sent in that direction from some -- towards some sheds or buildings from which the fire came, so the army used tanks to return that fire. And up there in Kozarac they started -- there were those people there. And as far as I can remember, there is a video, there is a tape showing how in Kozarac they had done something else, that they had set up a barracks of sorts or something there. And from what I heard afterwards, there was some terrorisation of their own people. They were requesting that everybody get weapons or to requisition livestock and other property. Many people refused to do that because -- I mean, Muslims, because some Muslims did want to go to war and others didn't. But whatever the case, the army went to respond to those operations of those soldiers in Kozarac, and that is when the conflict ensued, and the pursuits were organised of those who had fired but then led to other problems. People panicked, started leaving Kozarac, and, well, I don't know whether that was in the morning or in the afternoon or sometime during the day and I don't know on which date exactly - was it the 25th or the 26th or the 27th of May - the late Simo Drljaca and the late Mico Kovacevic called me, and I was at school or perhaps I was at home, so I just don't know -- I don't remember the date -- and asked know organise the reception of these people and those who came from Hambarine, but those were very few, and those who had started leaving Kozarac. They even asked me to organise that in the school building I was even angry with them, "Why are you involving me in this? There is the army. It has its command." But they were asking me to do it and both were also using the interphone [As interpreted] and I was using my own phone so that I could hear them talking with other people and because other people know me too, I am an old Prijedoran, and I knew lots of people, I was a teacher there, I grew up there, the whole town knew me, so that perhaps that is why it will be good if I try to organise it. And they asked me to accommodate those people in my school, but I refused that. Naturally. How can we put up those people who are sorts of refugees? How can we put them up in the school? So that many of them went to the Mladost gym. And meanwhile, people from the Red Cross came, and they were all ethnic origins, and they looked after those people. But then the report came that a large number of people were living Kozarac in their vehicles, trucks, cars, tractors, horse carts, trailers, and even on foot or with wheelbarrows or what do I know, and they asked me to go there to see them and try somehow to receive those people. Well, I was angry, but what can you do? That fell to my lot. So I went to see what was happening. And after all, it wasn't far from the town, and then I could indeed see that there were large numbers of people, women, small children, and so on, arriving in all those means of transportation, and I took along with me people from the Prijedor Red Cross, and there were women and men of all ethnic origins. And I remember, for instance, Rifit Kurtovic was my colleague. We worked in the school together. And then there was this Mrs. Jogic. I can't remember her first name. And we started helping those people to somehow get accommodated in the houses around the school. But the wave of people grew larger by the time, and then I asked the school caretaker, the man who looked after the school, to open the school so that we could put those people in the school, and they were put in the school and I think the next day or the day later people from the UNHCR and the International Red Cross arrived and brought powdered milk and whatever they could for children. I can't really remember what that person's name was from the Red Cross, but I think they came the next day or the day after. And two or three days later they asked that more care be taken of those people, more than hitherto, that some certificates be issued to them to show that those people were there, because that would be in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, that none of these people could be taken away somewhere, that nobody could take them away, and that is what we did every day. One could, of course, ask what was my role in that, because I wasn't a soldier, I wasn't an army officer, I wasn't the Red Cross, and I was all that at one and the same time. That is, I asked the commander in the barracks to send some troops to guard those people to avoid any attacks on them from Serb villages, that is, Petrov Gaj, which are right next door, and the first or the second day a policeman was killed there while those people were still trying to organise their -- to put up there, because fire had been opened from a railway carriage, from the railway station, which is some 50 metres or so away from the school. So my request was really justified. Somebody had to guard it, because people came there from individual units with their commanders and they organised those guards, and I looked after the food for those people and they also talked it between themselves and they would slaughter an ox or a cow to feed those people and they also asked the army to take two big soup kitchen facilities so that they could prepare their meals themselves there. And that was done and a number of lunch parcels were brought by the International Red Cross and the UNHCR and two large water tankers came for 1.000 or, I don't know, 2.000 litres of water with the hoses that could be turned into faucets, and there was a pump in the school yard and in houses nearby so that those people, those Muslims who were put up in houses nearby, they were living there, and towards Trnopolje they were living in all those houses rather far away. And since people needed also some green stuff, that is, cabbages, or people would call it, that is, carrots and parsley and kale and whatnot, those people could go around kitchen gardens in neighbouring houses and pick that, and nobody stopped them from doing that, except that people had to guard them, because the fighting was still going on. Later on it came to be known as cleansing. But by and large nothing special was happening and those people could move about freely and do all that. I don't know. Perhaps something is not quite clear, because I gave my statement in Banja Luka once, but there were no fences there except the hedge, that is, the common school fence, and there was also one which separated the cultural centre from the farmers cooperative, and that was 8 or 9 metres long, and that was a metal fence which I think had two lines of barbed wire on top. And then it turned out to be a camp or something. That was no camp at all. It was simply a necessity. And fortunately it was a place where people in predicament got together and the International Red Cross or the UNHCR brought a plaque which said "open centre." Nobody ever called it a camp, and I personally never saw it as a camp. Not that it wasn't a camp. It was one of the safest places in Prijedor and around because nobody could get into it and attack them. On one occasion some villagers, some local people, entered, and I think some women - I believe four of them were raped - otherwise, in that centre there were physicians all the time. I think two physicians, two Muslims, and there were also nurses there. And in daytime a doctor and a male nurse would come whenever it was necessary for them to do something. From what I know, people were taken to the hospital in Prijedor, those rapes, to try to establish, and I think only one of them was actually raped. And after that there was nothing, unless of course those who were there, perhaps there were some problems between them, but nobody was killed there. Perhaps some were around Kozarac, but that was some 7 or 8 kilometres away from there, and that was not my job because I had too many other problems to solve, to feed all those people, to look after them. It was very hot, and fortunately because there were two physicians from amongst the Muslim people and those others, we had no outbreaks of any epidemics, the water was not contaminated, but there wasn't enough room there. I mean, in the school and houses around it there were simply not enough room. So I asked those people from the building company gave me -- well, we call it the -- those steel rods that one uses for reinforced steel, and we used them to pitch some tents there so that people could be put up there too, seeing that it was so hot. I don't know what else to tell you. Simply -- well, anyway, people asked to leave and they left. They would organise themselves because at that time across Bosnia-Herzegovina there was fighting and many combat operations, and it simply turned out that every people aspired to join their own flock, as we say it, so that there were a number of people who wanted to go to Zenica, and on two or three occasions we organised the transport from there by train, so people left, a vast number of those who wanted to go went. And there were also those who didn't want to go because -- in other directions because their relatives or their friends or their neighbours had gone somewhere and they wanted to join them. But otherwise, they wouldn't have left. And then there were people from Travnik, from Zenica, from Doboj, because in Trnopolje there was a telephone -- I mean, those of the Red Cross had the telephone and of course the UNHCR, I mean, when they come they would have one with them. So they called up to say that they had got safe and sound wherever they were going and that those who were working there from the Red Cross said that they would enable families to get back together again. And once -- I don't remember whether it was June or July -- the UNHCR organised that the departure of some, I believe, 1400 -- 1.450 men to Karlovac. Now, was it -- with some ideas that not the UNHCR or the International Red Cross happy? I don't know. But there was the promise that the remainder, their families, those who were staying behind in Trnopolje at that time would have actually joined them. Later on one could hear in the town that the Red Cross and the UNHCR were organising without any problems and it would be easy for people to go either to neighbouring countries and further on abroad and then huge pressure ensued there in Trnopolje of people who wanted to leave, who wanted to leave Prijedor, until they understood that it would all come to nothing, and several other convoys went via Travnik. I asked the president of the executive community to provide transport, and the chief of the SUP to provide security for that transport. Some people took buses, some large lorries, they were escorted by the police. Unfortunately on one occasion - I can't remember exactly when - the police -- well, I don't know how to call that, but what they did was disgraceful for my people. Because of base instincts for the sake of looting - and this is something that I found out two or three days later - for these reasons they killed a number of people. I don't know how many, but they forced them to get off the buses before they crossed over into Travnik. I later found out about what had happened. But before that, and after that, it never happened. But on that one occasion, it did happen for the sake of looting, for the base instincts, that some people of my people had. After that, they went perhaps once or, what, twice again. Not many people remained, but people started coming from the town who hoped that through the UNHCR and the International Red Cross they'd be able to reach foreign countries in Europe. These hopes came to nothing. One of the presidents of the international office in Banja Luka, someone called Midjon [phoen], I think, one day he said that it would come to nothing, they were coming to Trnopolje, and then requesting that they be taken all over Europe and so on. I don't remember whether it was in mid-September or the first half of October. I don't know exactly, but it wasn't possible to do this. It was autumn already. It had started raining. I didn't consult anyone or ask for anyone's opinion, but I quite simply made those people leave Trnopolje. I said it was enough. And the people from the International Red Cross said that there was no longer reason -- any reason for them to be fed, they should return home. So I don't know how this should be put. This was never a camp. These were just the circumstances that prevailed, the unfortunate circumstances that were all -- that we all found ourselves in. There were some problems after all, but perhaps the late Simo and Mico did right. Perhaps it was good for someone like me to be there. Someone had to do this, and perhaps my authority, my respectability was used, and this finished in a humane way after all because there were quite a few pupils of mine, friends, acquaintances, et cetera. So perhaps there are a lot of things that I haven't mentioned and I don't know, but that's how this came to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. We, of course, have to come back to some details later. For technical reasons, we have to have a break now. The trial, therefore, stays adjourned until five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Kuruzovic, we are grateful that you gave us this overview from the beginning of 1992 until October 1992, but we have to go into some details now. First, may I ask you, what was the role of Kozarski Vjesnik after the takeover? Was it the official organ of the SDS, the official organ of the municipality, the official organ of the Crisis Staff, or how would you describe the role of Kozarski Vjesnik at that point in time, not before and not later. We learned that you worked with Kozarski Vjesnik later. But if you could describe, especially the role of the leading persons of Kozarski Vjesnik, Mr. Mutic and others.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Kozarski Vjesnik wasn't the official organ of the municipality or of the Crisis Staff. I think it was a limited company. I think it was an independent newspaper. But at the meetings of the executive committee and other bodies, as far as I know, they were attended by a journalist from Kozarski Vjesnik, by Mile Mutic, who was the director of Kozarski Vjesnik at the time, Rade Mutic, a journalist, Zivko Ecim, Milanko Rajlic, both journalists. So I don't know. I don't think it was - how should I put it - it wasn't an extension of a party or of organs of power or of the power structure at the time. Since there was a war in Western Slavonia, I know that they reported from there, being journalists, and there was a regular presence at the meetings of the organs of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mutic also attend meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mile Mutic did. I was at those sessions of the Crisis Staff very rarely because of the duties I had which regarded feeding, providing the police and soldiers with food, and issuing certificates for fuel. I had to be present there all the time. But I know that Mile Mutic did attend sessions and Milenko Rajlic, but how this proceeded exactly, I don't know. There must be some sort of records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Were there any other journalists present during the meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, as far as I can remember, I was there very seldom, but I think that Rade Mutic and Zivko Ecim were there. But how, to what extent, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's turn now to the role of the Official Gazette of Prijedor Municipality. Why was it that since the takeover the Official Gazette of Prijedor Municipality was edited as a gazette of year 1, even though we know that the Official Gazette of Prijedor Municipality existed for years already?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me a lot. I never saw that gazette, but I assume that it is because the Serbian Municipal Assembly was formed, and from that time onwards, from the time of its establishment, they decided to start by using number 1. I'm not sure of this though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown the cover page of document S180. Please put it on the ELMO. You can -- or maybe it's better we make use -- you get the B/C/S version and the -- the other one is on the ELMO. So you can see at the left-hand side "year 1." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come back to this document a little bit later. Mr. Kuruzovic, when to the best of your recollection you heard about the first plans of implementing a Crisis Staff in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that was, I don't know, two or three days after the takeover of power. It's hard to talk about that Crisis Staff in terms of it being a special body because all the members of the executive committee were members of it, all those who were part of an executive power, apart from the president of the municipality and the vice-president of the municipality. So there was the president of the municipality and the vice-president. If you need the names, Stakic was the president, Kovacevic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down and repeat the names.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the SUP was Simo Drljaca; the Chief of Defence and so on. That was the executive committee. The executive authority and the municipal assembly, and then there was the president and the vice-president of the municipalities, as far as I can remember. That was two or three days after the takeover of power, on the 29th, that is to say, on the 30th. I don't know who ordered this formation. I assume it followed the chain of subordination from the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or from the staff, from Banja Luka. I don't know exactly. I think that a statute of the municipal assembly was adopted. Maybe it was on the basis of the statute. I don't know exactly. As I said, I was present at those meetings very seldom and I didn't really pay attention to these official matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You yourself were a member of the Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. By virtue of my office as commander of the staff of Territorial Defence. But as I said, that wasn't a military formation really. It was more care for feeding the people, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And who told you that from now on the Crisis Staff was established and invited you for the first meeting of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I can't remember exactly, but assume it was the president, Stakic, or one of his associates, the Secretary of the Municipality. What was his name? Dusko, I think, Baltic or one of the officials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And when did you attend for the first time a meeting of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. A few days after the 30th of April. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One, two, three days, five days?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps. Perhaps three days. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, wasn't the word "Crisis Staff" already used some days before, already during takeover?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know for sure, but I don't think so. But the Crisis Staff, as I said, there was the one in the ARK Krajina and even in local communes, because the time was such, it was a crisis. Of course not only in parts of the town or the parts of local communes, not only -- this didn't only concern the Serbian population but the other population too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How often would the Crisis Staff meet as you said, two or three days after the takeover in the following period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that in the municipal assembly, I think there was a meeting of the executive committee every day and at the same time that was a Crisis Staff, because vital problems were being dealt with every day. Although, I would usually just say that I was there and then I would go to the command where I performed the duties that I mentioned, or I would be present for a very short period of time, because by virtue of my offices I didn't work in the municipality on a report of any kind. I couldn't influence decisions of any kind. This had to do with vital questions that related to organising life in the municipality, that is to say, in the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be your testimony that only in the first days of May the Crisis Staff met and more or less, nearly every day, as it was with the executive committee; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But after a very short period of time I think that was it was renamed the Presidency. I don't remember when that happened exactly. Maybe 10 or 15 days later. I don't know exactly. I can't remember. And the meetings of that body, well, I can't remember. I was present perhaps on one or two occasions very briefly, because on the 17th of May there was an order stating that I should become attached to the brigade, so I didn't have any particular links to the Crisis Staff, that is to say, to the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You testified that you participated only on limited occasions when you were present at a meeting of a Crisis Staff, who chaired the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the municipal assembly, Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who invited and where were these meetings held?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no particular kinds of invitations. It was a sort of working meeting, so to speak. Colleagues would meet in the morning because that was the purpose of the executive committee and meetings were held in the Municipal Assembly in Prijedor, in the building of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was it in a special room or one of the offices of the vice-president or what do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was down below. What's it called? In the basement of the municipal assembly where the canteen was, where they make coffee and tea. Because everyone when they -- when all the people turned up for work, they were down there, and there was an area next to that part and at the beginning they held several meetings. I can't remember how many exactly. And later on they were held -- well, there is an area next to the office of the president of the municipal assembly. It's still there, and meetings are still held there, meetings which were attended by a relatively low number of people. The current president of the municipal assembly, Murharem Murselovic, still holds meetings there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there, as it is often in political circles, an inner circle within the Crisis Staff, or were all members of the Crisis Staff on an equal footing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say. As far as I know, everyone was equal when discussions were held. But I assume that there were certain -- there was advice or agreements which were reached between the president of the municipality, the vice-president of the municipality, the president of the executive committee, the vice-president of the executive committee, so between the main people and perhaps those who were involved in the security for the town. That would be natural as a sort of preparation. But when this took place, how this took place, et cetera, I don't know, because I didn't attend such meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who would be those people, as you call it, involved in the security for the town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the Secretariat of the Interior that was involved in security for the town, and the chief, Simo Drljaca, was in charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there also a representative from the military present during those meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, very seldom. Although, I was there seldom too. As far as I know, that was -- on one or two occasions when I was there, that related to supplying food for the army. It related to vital issues, as far as I know, military subjects weren't discussed. I don't think that there was any particular kind of cooperation between the Crisis Staff and the military with regard to that matter. I don't think that they did anything together, apart from tackle vital issues, because there were problems relating to the electricity supply, the food supply, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And who would be the representative of the military when participating?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, on the two or three occasions that I was there, it was either Colonel Arsic or I don't remember what his rank was, Major Zeljaja or Ranko Rajlic, one of them, because they would come to request aid, fuel aid, aid with regard to electricity, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is a fact that we were not present. Of course, we are interested to know how was the procedure within the Crisis Staff, who prepared the agenda, who took notes, was there a voting or -- could you please tell us a little bit about this procedure. When you came together, how did it work?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I've just told you. It's a kind of daily work of this executive board. They were all together there, and I suppose that meetings were prepared by people in charge of individual areas of work. So they could work. The meetings were chaired and moderated by the president of the assembly, or that is, the Crisis Staff, Dr. Stakic. And what was the last part of your question? Oh, yes, I remember. Yes. I believe that notes were taken and the note taker was Spiro Marmat. He worked for the municipal authorities, and I believe he was the one who took notes, or at times Bosko -- excuse me, Dusko Baltic, who was the Secretary of the Municipality. I think he did at times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there a formal voting procedure?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember that. It was mostly discussions about various things that had to be done. If I was there, I'd ask Travar or the president of the executive board to provide fuel, to provide the vouchers, to procure food for the checkpoints, for people who were there on duty every day and every night, and such like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there ever a strong dispute on certain issues that you had to vote, or was it more or less unanimously?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I -- now I can't remember that. I don't remember any particular voting because there were people who were -- understood the problems of the town, and I think the decisions were the product of their mutual agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Page 39, line 18 you said today when we asked about the Crisis Staff, "It's a kind of daily work of this executive board." Would this mean that the executive board was -- could be equaled with the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, technically I think yes, except that alongside these members of the executive board there were also the president of the municipality and the vice-president of the municipality also participated in the work of the Crisis Staff. As far as I know, that was ex officio. Whether that office would be called the office of the commander of the Crisis Staff or the head of the Crisis Staff or the president, I can't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to present once again document S180 to the witness, and the English version on the ELMO, please. Mr. Kuruzovic, you can see this decision taken, as it reads here, the 20th of May, 1992 on the organisation and work of Prijedor Municipal Crisis Staff. Was this now a new Crisis Staff or was this only a declaration on the already existing Crisis Staff you mentioned beforehand?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I guess it's this letter thing, that it was, I suppose, pursuant to some legal regulations emerging from the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is why it was declared official.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But for you as a member of the Crisis Staff we learned that you -- to your other obligations you didn't participate very often. But was there any change on or about the 20th of May or, say, the 17th of May - you mentioned this day beforehand - in the work of the Crisis Staff, or was it the same procedure as beforehand?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. The decision ordered me to resubordinate myself to the barracks, that is, the brigade commander. After that, I don't remember if I was ever present at the Crisis Staff. But at one -- after one of the meetings of the Crisis Staff the official decision of the Crisis Staff was taken to disband the Territorial Defence staff to relieve me of my duty as its commander and that this whole command should be placed under the army command, and I think that it was decided - I don't remember exactly - but I think it was on the 29th of May or thereabouts, that decision. But when was it actually adopted, that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My question was: Did you see any new development within the work of the Crisis Staff during that period you attended meetings of the Crisis Staff? Was there something special? Was there a change? Was there an exchange of participants or whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think that work continued as it was before. I don't remember any particular changes. Perhaps there were some, but I was very seldom present there, so it wouldn't be honest to say something that I don't know. I don't recall exactly. I think that while I was present there that the system of work did not change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One additional question: Was there any special building of the -- of or for the Crisis Staff in Cirkin Polje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no building there. There was a building which until that time, that is, until the 17th, housed the Territorial Defence headquarters when I did my job. But later on, when the decision was taken, when the order was issued for resubordination, it was then said that it was being transformed into the -- into a logistics base. That is what it was called. But it continued doing what it did before, that is, providing food and all the rest that those checkpoints needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was it also the place where petrol vouchers were issued?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who issued these petrol vouchers? Was it the municipal assembly or was it the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: It was the municipal assembly, but its name -- that is, that the name of the president of the executive board in order to avoid crowding in the municipal hall, because that building houses many other services and that is why I was asked to do it, because it would be less crowded there. And I did it very honestly. I mean, people who had their companies, Muslims, and every other ethnicity, came, took those certificates, except that they really couldn't get as much fuel as they wanted, that is, I mean, they could not buy all the quantities they wanted, but as much as was available there. But no discrimination -- there was no discrimination. The municipal drivers and from all the other institutions came there to get those certificates and be issued vouchers to be able to buy fuel. There were two young women there who kept books, and I talked with those people and naturally they always asked for more fuel than we could realistically provide, so that we cut it down, and with that they went to the petrol station and paid for the fuel with their own money and that is how it went on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could one read at the entrance door of the building that this was a building where also the Crisis Staff was located?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, I don't remember that it had a name. People simply knew that. That's where it was. And they came and it was down the grapevine how people learnt it. Now, you've really caught me by surprise because I think that everybody knew the Crisis Staff was in the municipality, unless they thought this Crisis Staff was in this neighbourhood community. Otherwise, I don't remember. I don't remember there was anything saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff continue to exist later on in Urije? For the parties I make reference to transcript page 7537 through 7537 -- 7535 through 7537. The Crisis Staff in Urije. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean, Urije is part of the town of Prijedor, a locality in it, a neighbourhood in it, and Cirkin Polje, this neighbourhood community from which the police started, this centre from which the police set out to take over the power, well, I don't know, it's two or 300 metres away from this building and this building is also about two or 300 metres away from the office of the neighbourhood community in Urije, and this area is called Cirkin Polje because there's the neighbourhood community there, some office some two or 300 metres away, but it's the same area. And over here, where the neighbourhood -- where the official neighbourhood community of Urije is, that is -- that was part of the Territorial Defence. I mean, the official, the state one, of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the police -- police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be correct that you regularly could be found in this location as well?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In those earlier -- in morning hours, I'd always be there at 7.00 because there was a lot of work, very many people came to ask for those fuel vouchers, so that is where I was as a rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So to be quite clear - because unfortunately, we had never a chance to go to Prijedor ourselves - what is the distinction between the building in Cirkin Polje and the building in Urije?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I fully understand your question, but I'll try to do that. Cirkin Polje is the neighbourhood community, and there is a club there, a centre which holds cultural events and so on and so forth, where people get together, and that is from where the police set out to take over power. Now, from that -- from the neighbourhood community building in Urije to that building there is a privately owned building where there was a private company which had to do with Slovenia, as far as I know, and that is a building where I was in and issued those certificates. And the office of the neighbourhood community in Urije is to the left or before that building, and it was in this cultural club and everything else in Urije. But the distances are very short, so that is it. So that there wasn't anything. So this is the difference. One was the office of the neighbourhood community in Urije. That is called Prijedor II. And everything is under that neighbourhood community, that one in Cirkin Polje, in Palanciste [phoen] and Puharska and these are all parts of that large neighbourhood or local community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to put on the ELMO the next decision in the Official Gazette Prijedor. And if you, Mr. Kuruzovic, could be so kind and have a look on the next document. This is now the printed version. We could also provide you with the original of this document. But if Madam Registrar could prepare the original version if needed or if need may be. But based on this we can read -- we have, I think, altogether established that there's a printing error as it's meeting of -- it should read: "20 May 1992 there was a decision taken on appointment to Prijedor Municipal Crisis Staff." And you can read number 1, as you mentioned, the president, Dr. Milomir Stakic, Mr. Savanovic, Mr. Kovacevic, and then for the post of member Slobodan Kuruzovic, commander of Municipal Territorial Defence Staff. Is it correct that in conclusion of your previous testimony this was more or less of a declaration of that what already existed since some days after the takeover? Would this be correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So to be -- to have no doubt at all, there was no change the 20th or the 22nd of May as regards your own duties as the commander of the Municipal Territorial Defence Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
