utterances.text: Well, at that time the disposition was signed on the 17th that I was being relieved of my duty as the commander of the staff and was to attach myself to the brigade, to the army. So I think this simply confirms something that was already in existence and that it was simply legalised in this way, because you know how it is with documents, they're always late. But this composition properly reflects what is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How long did you attend meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember exactly. I know that it was seldom. Whether I ever came after the 20th, I don't know. Perhaps I did. Because that Territorial Defence staff became something else and because of this care, procurement of food, and those checkpoints and all that was necessary, I probably did come after that but not as a member any longer. But after this 20th or the 29th - I don't know exactly - there was an order to abolish the Territorial Defence staff and to relieve me of duty. I mean, that was decided earlier. But the document in writing I think was on the 29th but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you participate in the meeting of the municipal assembly on the 20th or the 17th - we don't know - of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: During one of the terms of duty I was a councilman in the municipal assembly representing my neighbourhood community, but as regards the date, I don't remember really and I don't know whether it was then or perhaps later. I don't remember. I mean, was it that year or one of the subsequent years? I don't remember any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, do you recall having given an interview on the takeover as it happened the night from the 29th of April to the 30th of April, a radio interview do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Radio Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A radio interview.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never gave any such interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we hear, please, the audiotape of Exhibit S91.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have copies if the booth would like copies of that transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Then let's wait a second, let the booth have copies of this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They were provided with copies during the break. Can they confirm they have it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we know the number of the page, please. Can we know the number of the -- the ERN number or something. We have a document, but we are unable to identify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It should be on the last page. It should read S91. Madam Registrar, may I have a copy, please, of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe the interview, if the tape is queued, with Mr. Kuruzovic begins on the page with the ERN number ending 723 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't know. We'll hear immediately. Maybe it starts already on 3721, where it reads, "Reporter." You've got it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the tape, please, be played.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] In the iron ore mine of Ljubija. Of course this is the programme we're talking about, the end of April 1992, that is the time when between the 29th and the 30th of April the Serb Democratic Party or, rather, the people from the Serb Democratic Party should take over all the most important offices in the territory of the Prijedor municipality, all the vital functions. One of the people who participated in all these activities from the beginning and in all the events between the 29th and the 30th of April, 1992 was Mr. Slobodan Kuruzovic, at that time the former commander of the TO in the town of Prijedor. And we'd like to greet him. Mr. Kuruzovic, this is the right moment to remember once again after Mr. Simo Miskovic that night between the 29th and the 30th and also to stretch our memory a little bit further into the past and recall some of the times. Slobodan Kuruzovic, as regards the political assessment and the situation Simo and Kurnoga, the current president of the municipality, have already said whatever there was to be said. I'd like to concentrate on the military aspect and to list things as they happened. Sometime around noon the notorious Jerko Doko from Sarajevo sent this official dispatch and with the Serbs should perhaps be grateful to him because of that, otherwise, we would have hesitated even more to do something that was extremely difficult to do since as Dusan Kurnoga correctly pointed out, each and every one of us placed our families in jeopardy since we had to do something which had never been done before and that was to seize power. And the situation was pretty clear, as plain as a pikestaff. As our people say, it was clear what they were up to and where they were going to do to us. We knew exactly their location, how they were armed, where and how they were trained in Kozarac, up there in Benkovac, Hambarine, and Puharska, we knew who bought the weapons and how they were organised, we knew it all. It was in the air. And Simo said earlier, this Jerko Doko helped us by sending this dispatch and they thought that the Serbs would never get hold of that dispatch and the Muslims were in power, but they were wrong. In 15 minutes this dispatch was in front of me. I read it and then we sat down and agreed on how we should proceed, as Simo said. At 5.00 we went to the barracks up there to discuss military tactics and decide what and when to -- what had to be done and when to do it. Dr. Stakic was there, the former president of the municipality, myself, Drljaca, Jankovic, and Cadjo, Miskovic as the president of the SDS and Lieutenant Colonel Arsic. Arsic was then the lieutenant colonel by the rank and he was the commander of the barracks and the commander of the 43rd Brigade. This group of people discussed this until nearly 7.00, and Arso then insisted and they decided that the moment was right. It had to be done right away with no special preparations since we had enough men at our disposal to prevent the massacre in the town. In that case, the consequences would be unforeseeable. Reporter: Before the 29th and the 30th of April, 1992 the Serb people tried in every possible way to prevent -- to preserve peace not only in the municipality of Prijedor but wider in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina by offering to the SDA various proposals for an agreement. What we are interested here and what our listeners would like to hear is if you can depict the atmosphere in that room where you were making this important decision between, let's say, 1400 or 1500 and 1700 hours. Kuruzovic: It is rather difficult to describe it. A moment ago I was about to say something in this regard. It was a difficult situation to do something like that. It was obvious that we did not hold any power either in Prijedor or in the republican level. It was such a large town and so many people who were not in agreement with us and the political problems concerning the division of power and all the other issues were dragging on for a year and a half and the situation was very complicated. However, the decision was taken and we agreed that the police should take over the power because together with Croats and Muslims they wore those blue uniforms and tried to maintain peace and order in the town and we decided that they should do it down here in the town, whereas the military aspect, that was under my command, should take care of that. In other words, that this takeover should be secured by the armed Serbs. Allow me to put things in chronological perspective. After that -- after we had agreed about that, sometime around 1900, Captain Bojic, Captain Savic, myself, and late Major Karlica we sat down and drew up a plan. We had everything in front of us, the whole town and the disposition -- and combat deployment of forces. It was no secret any more. We knew exactly where they had their men and their units. They even had arms, et cetera. At 2100 of course it was on the 29th. I summoned all the commanders of the regional staffs in our town, both from urban, suburban area, settlements, and villages. They went to that building of the Slovenian company in the field in Cirkin Polje where later the HQ of the Serbian TO staff was established and whose commander I was. I had been officially appointed by the Serb Municipal Assembly and we agreed on how to proceed and the mobilisation was ordered for 2.00 a.m. All armed Serbs in the localities, suburban areas, and villages were supposed to take their positions at a given moment. We agreed on the matter how it should be done. They had to be ready to enter the town strictly upon my order at 4.00 in the morning if need be and that's how it was. In the meantime, Simo, Dule Jankovic, Cadjo, of course there were many more of them, Marko Dzenadija, Jankovljevic, Pop Mudrinic, and let me not list all of them, but there were all those people from the police who did a lot of work. This reserve police force came to the community centre in Cirkin Polje. We -- some 260 men were called up but many more appeared, and the hall was packed. People talked and smoked. Nobody made any noise or shouted. I have no words to describe this atmosphere that reigned in that room. People were aware of the seriousness of the task ahead of us and they acted according to the situation. At 4.00 in the morning, the first convoys, so to speak, of men who were organised and tasked with taking over all the vital buildings and functions in the municipality set off this small mini-bus at Mico Janjetovic from Dragusko [phoen] locality, used to take the Rudar players to the soccer matches in, was used and the -- and that they went to the SUP, the court, the municipal building, Kozarski Vjesnik. This perhaps all sounds funny, but the last building to be taken was the public auditing service because the guard there who was a Serb had fallen asleep and I vividly remember how we sat in that room, Simo, Dule Jankovic, Cadjo, myself listening to the men talking on the Motorola, whether they should break into the door or not. And someone said, "Why bother breaking in. He'll wake up eventually." And that's what happened. So there were no incidents, nothing. And at 4.25 the last report came through. The procedure was quite simple. One could just say "over," and that was a sign that the task had been completed, that is, that a certain office that Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 14479 to 14487. is, that its function had been taken. At 5.00 the representatives of our Serbian authorities came to me to the headquarters, the president of the municipality, the vice-president of the municipality, the chairman of the executive committee, secretary for economy, Defence Minister, and all the others according to their respected departments and municipality and then we began dispatching them. There were also a few prominent general managers there. There's no need for me to name them all. They went to their respective offices. Where armed our policemen waited for them with the lists of people who would not be allowed to enter the municipal buildings. The court, the police, and so on and so forth, that is, Simo just mentioned it and I think it was good -- it was really fortunate that it occurred to us, for instance, the president of the municipality could not go in, the chairman of the party could not go in, and some other top officials and supporters of the SDA could not enter, when all the others, that is, Muslims or Croats, regardless of nationality and regular employees, clerks, and all the rest, they went to work as usual. The only difference being that the Serb flag and the Yugoslav flag were hoisted up on the municipal building to mark that the takeover had been carried out. By 6.00 it was all over. We informed Vojo Kupresanin in Banja Luka. At that time it was still the AR Krajina since everything had been not been done yet. He did would not believe when we told him that it was over and that we have seized the power in the municipality since it was much more difficult to do it here than in those small towns like Novi, Dubica, Sana. Because it was well known we were a large regional centre and the chief of this regional centre was Mirza Mujadzic, since Simo had already said everything about him. There is no need for me to repeat it. Reporter: Since this action to seize power in the municipality had been meticulously planned or carried out without a single incident or shot being fired, we would like to know what the assessments were that afternoon on the 29th. Did you expect an immediate reaction on the part of the SDA and what would have been your course of action in such a case? Kuruzovic: It is very difficult to answer the first part of the question with regard to their possible reaction. I do not know if the time is right to discuss all that. But we knew that that they had been armed we knew where they were, we knew where their strongest units were locate. But there was something else about which they did not pay attention all that time. As Simo said, as we were trying to democratic option and trying to draw their attention to the fact that they shouldn't proceed in that way, later that month -- maybe it's not okay that I say that as a general manager of our company, but we will talk about what happened during that month in Prijedor. We were fighting in Western Slavonia. We'd been fighting in Western Slavonia for a year: They hadn't. And that was our enormous advantage since we knew that they did not stand a ghost of a chance to do something so drastic and eventually it proved right when 120 of them carried out that attack thinking that they could do something using their rifles, and you know how this attempt ended. Our assumption was that -- well, we predicted that nothing silly would happen, in other words, that they might cause an incident because in each and every Serbian village, in every part of the town of Prijedor, in every suburban settlement where the Serbs lived everything had been organised. Reporter: Were you much surprised by the attacks which ensued on the 29 or 30 May when the Muslims, the Muslim fanatics of the SDA, attacked the town of Prijedor? Kuruzovic: We expected something like that any day because we knew that they could not get over that, our people will proudly remember that and theirs as well, although they will judge it different. We simply outsmarted them and seized power in 25 minutes without firing a single shot because we did not want it to happen in any other way. Let me take this opportunity to say and remind you that even before that there were many problems. There were burglaries, robberies, et cetera, in the town, and that was one of the compelling reasons for us to attempt to prevent that. They did not surprise us because we knew they did not have respectable forces, but I was personally surprised a little bit because this Slavko Acimovic was my pupil. I could not believe it. He was something of an enigma. We knew he had been plotting something and that he was a member of the HDZ, but that he was capable of something like that was something that was beyond my expectations. I know why that happened. We talked a lot about that later on. They did not want that much to seize power. Their intention was to excuse themselves before their own people. Alija is doing something similar at the moment. He constantly attacks and reports casualties. Let me not mention all of it now. But for instance, the Markale incident or the French being killed, et cetera, et cetera, merely proves that something is being done. Maybe it's not fair to talk like this, but I know that they took a hell of a lot of money from their people in order to procure weapons to attack the Serbs, slaughter them and eventually cause an exodus. We struggled for a month to persuade them to disarm and hand in those weapons, to resolve all the problems, preserve peace, and schedule elections. We don't care who wins. To preserve peace and order in the town, but to no avail. Of course, in the case they would have to return the money to the people. Reporter: This is a good occasion to make a parallel at the end of our conversation and to compare the SDS then in April 1992 and now in April 1995. Kuruzovic: I don't know if I should be the one to comment on this, but I can say that at the time the party was highly organised, aware of everything, and prepared for anything. As a member of the SDS, myself and the others, our president, Simo, we all had to, as our folk would say, muster courage and every one of us was ready for that. And now we are facing difficulties and the reasons for this are many, pressures from the outside world, the fact that we are misunderstood by our brothers on the other side of the Drina River, and then there are a lot of problems here among us, so I would say that the reason for some of the problems, the existential problems that exist, I hope that everything might be solved, God willing, once this state of ours is stabilised and I hope that everything will eventually be all right. Reporter: This is Prijedor Radio, live broadcast from the Red Auditorium, the Crvena Sala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please let's have a short break, let the French -- no, no. We'll stay here, only that the French booth can catch up. [Interpretation] Thank you very much. That's all. [In English] Do you recall now this interview with Radio Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. At the time I was the director of Radio Prijedor, and this interview was conducted by Zoran Baros. When you asked me, I thought you were asking me about an interview from 1991, 1992, 1993. I know that I didn't give any interviews at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So the reporter mentioned here would -- on this would be Zoran Baros. And you recall the exact date when you gave this interview?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I don't remember. I assume it was in 1995, perhaps, when power was taken over, but I'm not sure. This is on the basis of the subject or the subjects discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Does this interview, your interventions, reflect that what happened in 1992 correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning - I think I said something to this effect - I took this to be a serious matter, and I know that I couldn't just say anything. The situation was quite problematic. The Muslim and the Croatian people were divided and prepared for everything. The Serbs were afraid of the consequences, afraid of what might happen, afraid that things might happen similar to what happened in 1942, so it is similar to what I have been discussing here since this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the page ERN number ending with 722, last line, you start saying, "As Simo said, 5.00 we went up there to the barracks to discuss military tactics and decide when and what had to be done. Dr. Stakic, former president of the municipality, myself, Drljaca, Jankovic, and Cadjo, Miskovic as the chairman of the SDS, and Lieutenant Colonel Arsic were there." What was it when you discussed "military tactics"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was on the 29th at about 1700 hours. We discussed the possibility of problems arising when taking over power and said that armed Serbs from the Territorial Defence should become involved from the entire municipality. But this didn't happen. There weren't any interventions. There weren't any incidents. Nothing happened. It was just a matter of providing security in case fighting broke out, to prevent anything unfortunate from happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So would the conclusion be correct that at that period of time you discussed the maybe event that Muslim forces would react and resist the takeover by military means? Did you discuss how to react by military means?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we didn't discuss it in that way. These people were there in their local communes, in the neighbourhood communities, and they were on guard, they were on duty, they were there over the night in case something happened. And then I assume it would have been necessary to intervene. But as far as the question as to whether we planned anything in this respect, no. There were just certain discussions that were held, if something unfortunate happened, discussions about how we were going to react. I don't know what this would have turned into. But there were no problems in the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's undisputed that no bullet was shot at all. But in preparing this takeover, you yourself mentioned the words "we discussed military tactics." Did you prepare some military platoons or other groups in case there would be military action taken by the other side how to react with military means? Would this be correct? Because I think it would be quite natural to -- when preparing a takeover also to take into account that there would be a reaction from the other side. So what does it mean "discuss military tactics"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you, but perhaps you have forgotten the fact that there were over 400 policemen there and it was agreed that they should be called up and as a result there was not a great risk. If there was some sort of reaction, I suppose that the police would be the first -- would have been the first to intervene. This was certainly taken into account. If people armed, people in the Territorial Defence, that is to say, Muslim units, Muslims and Croats who were armed on a private basis in case something happened, in such a case one would probably have reacted. But as far as a plan is concerned, there was no particular plan. We simply discussed this subject. In such a case I assume it would have been necessary to ask for help from the command, from the army, from the brigades. But there weren't that many soldiers there either. There were few soldiers in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I take it that you came to the conclusion that your power, especially police power, was that overwhelming that there was in your assessment no major risk of any response by the other side. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think so, because there was no other objectives. The only objective was to take over the functions of the president of the municipality, the vice-president of the municipality, the director of the post office, the chief of the SUP, et cetera. Nothing else had been planned. We hadn't planned to exert pressure on the people. No such things had been considered. As I said, all the others who worked in any of these other institutions, they appeared at work and worked as they had previously done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's now turn to page ERN number 72492. There it reads, "We decided that they should do it down here in the town, whereas the military aspect, which was under my authority, should be taken care by us." Could you please explain this sentence given in the interview by you that the military aspect was under your authority.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's because I was the commander of the Territorial Defence staff. But otherwise, everything was organised in such a way that there were defence units in local communes. And if something happened, they were there. But how should I say it? It wasn't really a military organisation in the strict sense of the term. It was just Serbians, the people, civilians who were armed. They were in the reserve forces because they had served in the JNA. We had all served in the army. They had uniforms. They had their duties. But these were forces from the Territorial Defence, the town's Territorial Defence, which existed at the same time as the Territorial Defence staff, the Serbian one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Apropos uniform, did you wear a uniform at that period of time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we wore uniforms, but many people didn't have uniforms. But usually, yes, that Territorial Defence had been mobilised and most of the men had uniforms and they were all positioned in those local communes throughout the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When was the first day you wore a uniform?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in June or August 1991. That's when the mobilisation was carried out on the basis of the advice of the defence for the municipality of Prijedor. These instructions concerned duty -- tours of duty. There were units in all the inhabited local communes, and it was under the command of the official staff of the Territorial Defence and it was under the command of Rade Javoric. All the units and all the local communes and in the town of Prijedor, Prijedor I, Prijedor II, and Prijedor III, as we call these area, Gomjenica, Tukovi, Dragotina, et cetera, in all these places these Territorial Defence forces were mobilised. And now I can't remember exactly whether it was in July or August. On one day there was a decision to distribute weapons. A few days before that there were instructions for duty, and then weapons and ammunition was distributed in all the local communes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How many persons were under your command in the Territorial Defence as of the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say. Quite a few people and no one, because, as I said, that Territorial Defence staff wasn't really functioning in the military sense. I never issued any military orders, and no one ever carried out military orders, apart from the ones I have mentioned, because at the same time that Territorial Defence staff existed and officially functioned in the municipality. Rade Javoric was in command. This was the regular body, and they were under his command. But if something happened I assume that I, cooperating with Javoric from the brigade command, would have tried to save the situation, prevent incidents and problems from occurring. But because there were so many policemen who participated in the takeover of power, this was not very probable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But once again, how many persons would you command at that time, together with your colleague, within the Territorial Defence, at a maximum?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. That's difficult to say. In the Territorial Defence command at the time -- well, there must have been records. I don't know. Perhaps 1.000. Perhaps there were 2.000. I don't know. But these are people of all nationalities in the field, in the entire municipality. But this was just a formal matter, my command of the Territorial Defence, because I was involved in other matters. This just sounded nice. Because at the same time I worked as the head of the school and I went to work every day and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In which way were these members of the Territorial Defence armed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence had its own weapons according to establishment. The weapons were in the barracks. And the commander, Javoric, organised the way in which this should be done, and I know that they used lorries to take away weapons into certain areas, to certain local communes, to units of the Territorial Defence, to all -- to Prijedor I, II, and III, to Kozarac, to Hambarine, to Omarska - weapons were taken there by these lorries - to Brezicani, to Puharska, et cetera. The population there is mixed. In some places the Muslims are the majority and in others are the Serbs. In Ljubija, et cetera, these places were all under the command of that staff. I can't remember now exactly whether it was in July or August 1991 when these weapons were distributed to all the Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What kind of weapons? Ranging from pistols to --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Infantry weapons, up to light machine-guns. Infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'll turn now to another issue. On the same page you're speaking about the meeting at Cirkin Polje. Do you recall whether or not new IDs were issued at this meeting in Cirkin Polje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: IDs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean IDs? For purpose of identification or -- I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the purpose of identification, that these persons were allowed to enter these buildings, the municipal building and so on, the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember any such IDs. And in my opinion it wasn't necessary, because everyone knew these people, regardless of what their nationality was. They knew everyone in the town. And the police or, rather, those people involved in providing security for those buildings, after the takeover of power, they were also familiar with these people. I don't think that there were IDs of any particular kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So was it then the other way around, turning now to page 725, where I can read, "They went to their respective offices where our armed policemen waited for them with a list of the people who were not allowed to enter municipal buildings." When did you compile these lists of people who were not allowed to enter the municipal buildings, the court, the SUP buildings, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: That -- I mean, it's not so important whether it was me or not. I didn't participate in that. But it was the policemen who did it, those who headed -- those who want to take over the power and then seek to guard those buildings. And it was all prepared by the late Simo, with Dule Jankovic, and Marko Dzenadija. And they said that the president of the municipality may not go in and those other officials - I can't remember now what their names are - and the same applied to the police station, to the court building, the president of the court, then the director of the post office, of the auditing office, and I don't know who else. I don't remember the names of those people who were directors or managers before that. But these people, say, for instance, the one who was the director of the auditing service, he could not get in, but all the others -- I mean, all the other employees could get in. Now, I don't know exactly how many of those officials there were - perhaps 10 or 12 - so this referred to some dozen people. All the others normally came and did the jobs that they had done before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So these lists of people who were not allowed to enter the buildings, they were already compiled or were they composed during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: They were compiled there, in the organisation when the power was taken over by the police. I wasn't present there. I was sitting over here. And it was only after 5.00 that those officials came and they were taken away from there in buses. So I know it from stories, what happened later on when it was over, that those policemen had the names of those individuals who should not be allowed access into those buildings, and that is how it all ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You continue then stating, "I think it is good that we luckily came to the smart idea that the president of the municipality, the chairman of the party, and some top officials, supporters of the SDA, were not granted access."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would include Professor Cehajic, that he wouldn't be allowed to enter the building of the municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: It is, yes. They made those lists, and that was good. At least, that is what I think. Now, it's another matter whether that is how it should have been done at that time, whether it was according to law and everything else. But that is how it happened, and fortunately there were no excesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the next page you state - line 4 - "We informed Vojo Kupresanin in Banja Luka." Who's we?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember exactly who it was that informed him, but one of those in that group who were sitting there. I think it was a deputy. He was a senator, Srdjo Srdic. I think he was the one who notified him. But I'm not too sure. I know they called Banja Luka to say that power had been taken over in Prijedor and that there were no excesses, gunfire, or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Why was it necessary to inform Banja Luka immediately at 6.00, early in the morning?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's hard for me to say. Mr. Srdjo -- but I think that he did it. He was a high-ranking official of the SDS. He was a member of parliament. And that is why he let them know that there were no problems in the municipality -- that there were problems in the municipality, that there were reasons to take over the power. And I suppose they were happy to hear that because no untoward things happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We have now to make another break. And the Trial Chamber stays adjourned until 2.00 sharp. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Kuruzovic, let's turn back immediately to your radio interview you gave. We discussed the question of the information of Mr. Vojo Kupresanin in Banja Luka. Wouldn't you agree that when you report to a person prior to this you got or people got a request from this person to report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So to be more concrete, was the takeover a decision taken on the level of Prijedor or was it a decision ordered from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was decided in Prijedor or -- maybe, but I don't know. But I've already said what was the chief reason and the day and why was that particular day selected. As for the rest, I really do not know whether there was something like that, whether there were some discussions to that effect. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The same page, next line, you continue saying, "At that time that was still AR Krajina, the Autonomous Region of Krajina, since everything had not been done yet." What does it mean "everything had not been done yet"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I spoke about that within the context of a different time, 1995, that is, when there was Republika Srpska in place, because before that it was called the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was an integral part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and now it's some kind of a special part set up as a republic of the Serb people, and I assume -- or rather, later on it transpired that that was the goal. But many things happened during the war, and I know that the Dayton Accords put in place a state with two entities, Republika Srpska, and the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would this be in line with that what we could hear later, the same occasion by -- in Radio Prijedor as it was expressed by the late Dr. Kovacevic when he stated -- if you want, you could -- we could listen to this, but I'll try to read out this. On page 729, the eighth line from the bottom, "Serbs must remain in a single state, not in this Serbian Krajina, Krajina, Serbia, Montenegro, and whatnot. It's all the same to me. That's a course that we had taken then, and I believe that the majority still adheres to the same principles. Otherwise, it wouldn't be good. I would not like to comment on the preparations any more. We had earlier formed the so-called shadow government." A shadow government, would this be the Serbian Assembly established the 7th of January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, one could put it that way. Officially there was the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor in Bosnia, and the Serb people elected its delegates and set up the Serb Assembly of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So the expression "shadow government" is not a strange expression for you and was not in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, one cannot call it a shadow government. The municipal assembly is the legislating body, and the term "shadow government" is used when there is the opposition to those who are in power and they set up another government, a counterpart government with its ministers, and so on and so forth, and that is called the shadow government. I learnt it about two or three years ago when the municipal authorities in Republika Srpska were elected. There was this thing, the shadow government, formed by the opposition, and it was spoken about publicly on television and so on. In Prijedor one cannot really speak about a government because there was the municipal authority which existed and then the Assembly of the Serb People was formed, and the assembly is not the executive branch of power, as far as I know. It is the legislative branch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So what was it that brought Mr. Kovacevic to saying in the same interview only a few minutes later, "We had earlier formed the so-called shadow government"? And he continues, "That is a political expression, although for us it was a government which had already been in function at that time. When we decided to do it, we did it the way we did it. We set up a staff."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. This is the first time I hear that this is what the late Mr. Kovacevic said. Perhaps that is what he meant. Perhaps there were some discussions conducted about it. But officially, no. To my knowledge, until that 29th of April there was never any talk about the takeover of power. It was simply that we, the people, were unhappy about the situation in the town, the establishment of the executive board of that power, and that is, the government, and many things were not really going smoothly, and as our people said, it was just one drop too many. When the army was ordered to be disarmed and that the barracks be taken over. And that was why the decision was taken to do it overnight, to reach that agreement and to take over the power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But what was the reason to establish the Serbian Assembly already the 7th of April -- the 7th of January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I guess that it was because of all those well-known developments, that the Serb people refused to be over voted as a minority in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, the pre-Dayton one. From what I remember seeing on television, the discussions led nowhere. There was -- they were constantly over voted. And I know that in the territory of this former Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Assembly of the Serb People in Bosnia-Herzegovina was set up and it was called the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Why does Mr. Kovacevic mention this connection also, not only Serbian Krajina, but also Serbia and Montenegro? Isn't it true, sir, that at that point in time the persons in office already aimed at forming a Serbian state, a one-and-only Serbian state?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that I do understand. Whether some preparations were being conducted, I do not know. But there was an aspiration and it was talked about for a long time as a solution of the Serb ethnic question. Perhaps it originated in Serbia, perhaps in these lands. Whether it was when the late Vuk Draskovic -- no, not Vuk Draskovic, sorry, Raskovic emerged -- so it's not Vuk Draskovic but Raskovic, and I forget his name -- yes, Jovan Raskovic. It was also the position of a number of parties in Serbia, and this need to solve the Serb ethnic question throughout was discussed. And perhaps then this was used and some started talking about the creation of a greater Serbia, but I do not agree with that, but however these -- this is my personal opinion. As far as I know, such policy did not exist. What was at stake was cooperation, agreement, economic cooperation, and after all it is respected today the cooperation between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia, that is, Republika Srpska and former Yugoslavia, now Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Finally aiming at the Greater Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that that is indeed so, but many people did aspire to that, and those people were listened to. Their thoughts were listened to. Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When exacting participation in this meeting and being elected in this meeting of the 7th of January, 1992, what was the reason justifying the attempt to replace the freely elected persons in the Municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, one of the reasons must have been what I have been talking about, that is, the situation. And perhaps it was also the aspiration and the policy that the Serb people should acquire its state in the territory of the former Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To continue on the same page ending 726, you discussed the events in Prijedor and you stated, "We fought in the Western Slavonia for a year and they did not and that was enormous advantage since we knew that they did not stand a ghost of a chance to do something so drastic and eventually proved right when 120 of them carried that attack thinking that they could do something using rifles, and you know how this attempt ended." By this 120 of them attacking you allude to the attack on Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So was it at that time your opinion that these 120 had not the slightest chance with their attack because of the overwhelming power of the Serbian side? Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct, because Serbs held the power in the town and it's true that a large number of Serb citizens in those brigades had been on the front in Western Slavonia, had gone through it, and presumably did not find those attacks too difficult to resist and so prevented it, so they couldn't cause more misfortune around the town, and that is how it ended, that only 16 Serbs were killed in the town and around it, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Muslims and Croats were killed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that I don't know. I don't know that. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then one final question related to your own interview: You mentioned that you had been a member of the SDS. Can you please tell us from which date on you were a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, but sometime as of spring 1991 or perhaps February or March. And it was no surprise, because there were already many problems in Krajina and West Slavonia, so that especially later almost all the Serbs belonged to that movement. Because it was not a political party, it was a movement which showed and said that they took great care of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Coming back to the Crisis Staff. When would you say were the first enactments passed by the Crisis Staff? Do you recall that later on they were endorsed or accepted by the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, the confirmation of decisions within the competence of the municipal assembly adopted by the Crisis Staff? When would you believe that these decisions started? Immediately after the takeover in the beginning of May; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, except that I don't remember those decisions. I saw it as part of the daily chores. Whether -- well, I suppose those -- that these decisions which were important for the Serb people were confirmed, were ratified by the assembly, but I do not know the dates when the assembly met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you receive the enactments or decisions of -- adopted by the Crisis Staff immediately after the decision, were they distributed by the staff members of Mr. Baltic to the members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't really remember that. Believe me. All I have is the decision on the relief of duty and resubordination to the brigade, the 43rd one, and that was done in writing. The rest, I know that notes were kept, but I had no opportunity to see the decisions in writing. It was usually kept in the archives of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. May I ask the usher to present in B/C/S document S250 to the witness and then please stay there with the English copy and the English copy be put on the ELMO. You can see this is one of -- confirmation of decisions, the 24th of July, 1992 and the enactments passed -- If we could see the bottom of the page, please. So just go through some -- go through some of the decisions. Enactment passed on the 29th of May, 1992. I'll ask you - and the same question is true for all the coming decisions - do you recall the discussion on these issues. Number 3, "Decision dismissing the Serbian Territorial Defence commander."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't present. At that meeting I only heard that it had been decided to dismiss it and then I received the decision. But I wasn't present. If the notes were taken, I suppose the minutes would show that I was not present there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And you said you heard about this decision. Did you also hear about the reasons why this decision was taken?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Why, I didn't. All I have is the decision on the dismissal of the commander, or rather, the relief of duty, and I received it on the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Number 4, "Determining that the Serbian Territorial Defence is no longer required." Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see the decision, but that's what it also says in that decision, I think, that I received, that there was no need any more for the Serb Territorial Defence, that is, staff was being disbanded and that I was being relieved of that duty. It was all written down in that decision, I think. I mean, in the decision of the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Coming now to the enactments passed on the 31st of May, 1992. Number 2, "Conclusion related to people fleeing in Trnopolje." Do you recall this? Because this would be in the area of your competence; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see what it says, "Conclusion related to people fleeing in Trnopolje prohibiting the return of POWs to Trnopolje and Prijedor." No, I never received a single one of these conclusions. I don't know what they refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to turn to the next page, please. Was there any decision taken to hinder persons from fleeing from Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of such a decision, and I don't know whether it was necessary for those who were there to flee. They were taken care of. Their health and their safety was taken care of. Perhaps some people did leave because there was no fences and there was no great need to prevent them from doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But why was it then that the Crisis Staff had to discuss the issue of fleeing people from Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, "to flee" means people -- it means the people who have problems go elsewhere for safety reasons. That's what the word means in our language. It means trying to avoid problems that have to do with the war. In Kozarac, there were such problems that appeared in Trnopolje too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We'll come back to this later. Then enactments passed on 3 June, 1992, "Conclusions for approving funds for the purchase of uniforms." Why was it for the Crisis Staff to purchase uniforms? Do you recall this decision or the conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't recall it. I can't see it here. I don't know when it was. What did you say, the 3rd of June?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 3rd of June, conclusion number 1.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I see. I see. "Approving funds for the purchase of uniforms." I'm not aware of that conclusion, but I do know that all the members of the Crisis Staff received uniforms, and I know that they even sent one to me, a uniform that was intended for the deputy Srdjo Srdic. It was enormous. He didn't want to wear it because he was also a senator, so I was given this uniform. It was a summer uniform made of thin material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was it the same kind of uniform you wore in your other capacity previously?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. This uniform was the so-called olive-grey uniform, the earlier one, and this one was a camouflage uniform, dark brown. It was a camouflage one. It wasn't green; it wasn't really a military one. It was more like a sports uniform. But it amounted to a uniform, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And did you at the same time receive a pistol?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dr. Stakic in uniform wearing a pistol?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I saw him in uniform, but I can't remember him carrying a pistol. But what's it called -- I wasn't present at the time, but what is it, a Heckler, something like that, a pistol which I had very briefly, and then I was requested to return it, which I did. But it was practical. It was easy to carry, but I never really needed it. I kept it in my car. I never took it out of the car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And let's go down on the same page. May I ask the usher, please, to stay with the ELMO and that we can change the -- first to the bottom of the page. Whenever you see a decision, conclusion you recall, please tell us. But in order to save time -- Could the usher now, please, turn to the next page. The enactments passed the 5th of June, 1992. Do you recall the order requesting the Serbian Territorial Defence to return its remaining receipts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember this order, that this was done. The Secretary for Economy was called and all those certificates were returned to the municipality, to the Secretariat for the Economy, and lists he took before, how many certificates he got to buy fuel, it all went to the municipality and they provided this in the municipality. It went to the Secretariat for Economy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So the conclusion would be correct that you don't recall this order but its implementation; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then number 8, "Order requesting the organs of Cirkin Polje local commune to vacate the premises of the former Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what -- that's what the people called it, the Crisis Staff. It only lasted for one night in those premises. But in the local commune of Cirkin Polje, the reserve police was present there. But when that was - I can see the date, the 5th of June - but that had all been vacated. Everyone had left those premises. And there were only people remaining in that house next to the local commune in Cirkin Polje. Some sort of logistics base had been formed there and they were involved in providing food for the police and for the troops, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So once again, you don't recall the order but its implementation; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's turn to the next page, please -- or first, let's have a view on -- you should have the chance to see the entire document, also on the bottom. And please in the English version the next page. You can see the conclusion number 20 -- under number 7, "20-111-153/92 on the duty to compile lists of soldiers for the purpose of procuring cigarettes." Why was it for the Crisis Staff to compile lists of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I haven't seen this -- I haven't seen this conclusion either. But I suppose it was to avoid trafficking with cigarettes. There were to be a certain number -- there was to be a certain number of soldiers in the barracks, and they were to have cigarettes distributed to them, and they probably were thinking of soldiers, policemen at the checkpoints so that they could all get cigarettes because this was an item of value. People smoked a lot. There weren't any cigarettes available, so they probably made an effort for the soldiers, for the members of the Territorial Defence, and for the police to be provided with cigarettes. I assume that that is only because of the number of cigarettes. It only concerns the number of cigarettes, not the compiling of some kind of lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to the next page in the English version. Enactments passed the 10th of June, 1992. Conclusion assigning the duty of providing security for the Trnopolje camp to the regional command." Do you recall this decision or conclusion and its implementation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the conclusion but its implementation, yes. With the assistance of the regional command, as I said, I was everything and nothing. I wasn't just a soldier or someone who had -- who was involved with the Red Cross. I was all things at the same time. I tried to provide security for the people in Trnopolje. I managed to do this by requesting that the command allow military units to be used, the size of one platoon, and they should rotate on a daily basis and protect the people. So this conclusion probably makes sense because it's demanding the command to provide security. When they would turn up, they all had unit commanders and they would be in charge of security. This was not my job. I was only an intermediary. And this was done well because the people were protected, in spite of the fact that there were certain incidents. But on the whole, everything was all right and the people were protected throughout this period, this lengthy period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How could it be that it was for the Crisis Staff assigning this duty to the regional command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I'm also a bit surprised, because this is a conclusion on assigning a duty. Because in my opinion, the Crisis Staff was not in a position to issue orders to the army. That was not the structure of subordination. But perhaps the person who compiled this -- well, perhaps some other word could have been used, but I can see that it mentions assigning duty, and I don't think that the Crisis Staff was in a position to issue orders to the army. They could have requested assistance. They could have requested that this be done, and it was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we have a look down to the bottom of the page, please. Please feel free if you want to comment on the one or other enactment. I would now turn to the enactment passed the 12th of June, 1992. Coming back to a previous question, "Reducing working hours at Kozarski Vjesnik in Prijedor." How is it possible that the Crisis Staff had the power to reduce working hours at Kozarski Vjesnik?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps the people from Kozarski Vjesnik requested that the hours be reduced. I don't know. Because as you know, in the organisation of the municipal assembly everyone had certain working hours. Working hours were allocated for theatres, for shops, for catering establishments, companies. One would have to work for eight hours, so you'd start at 7.00 or 8.00, I don't know. But why it mentions reducing hours here, I don't know. Reducing the working hours at Kozarski Vjesnik in Prijedor, I don't know. Perhaps it was at their request. That's all I can think of. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Wouldn't that mean in conclusion that Kozarski Vjesnik at that point in time was subordinate to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I don't know. I don't remember that there were orders of any kind as to how one should work, who should work and when, unless there were certain communiques that were important for the people, that is to say, for the citizens in the town. Then any media establishment would be obliged to provide such information. But about the working hours, no, I don't believe so and I don't think it was under the patronage of the Kozarski Vjesnik. I think it was -- as far as I know, the Kozarski Vjesnik was a limited company. And later on a decision was taken that Kozarski Vjesnik was a public company, that is to say, that the municipal assembly had to be concerned with its finances, the legislative organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When did this happen, the change?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I know that this change occurred, but I don't know when exactly. Perhaps it was in 1993 or in 1994 in the spring, something like that, because when I became the director of Kozarski Vjesnik it was on the 5th of May, I think, the first days of May in 1995. And at the time Kozarski Vjesnik was a public company. But the employees in Kozarski Vjesnik never really accepted this, so this matter has still not been fully solved to this day, the matter as to whether it's a public company or a limited company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's turn, please --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: A shareholders company, a limited company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- to the next page in the English version, starting with the stop. In case you would see an enactment you want to comment on -- stop. I want to draw your attention to the enactment passed on the 16th of June, 1992. Number 1, "Conclusion assigning members of the Crisis Staff. The duty of preparing a system of supplying food to the army and police troops." Do you recall this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall this conclusion, but I understand what is at stake. The person who wrote this probably made an error when he said "assigning members of the Crisis Staff." This can only relate to the Secretary for Economy or the Secretary of Finance or to both of them, so that they could help to provide food, to help supply this, to help with preparing the food for the army or the police. It can't be an assignment to all the members of the Crisis Staff. This hasn't been correctly put. But I think that I am right and what I have said is correct. I think it refers to the president of the executive committee or, rather, to the Secretary for the Economy and the Secretary for the Finance of the municipal assembly, that is to say, of the executive committee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was this conclusion implemented or were the army and the police troops supplied --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: For sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's turn to the next page, please, the enactment of 17 of June, 1992. Number 1, "Order concerning the formation of a single intervention platoon." Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember this. I wasn't in the municipality at the time. I don't remember this order. But I think I know what it's about. It's a police unit which is part of the Secretariat of the Interior in Prijedor, or rather, the centre of public security. That must have gone from the Ministry of the Interior at the republican level and then down the chain of subordination, and then turned up as an order for the formation of an intervention platoon. This is what I assume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What was the purpose of such an intervention platoon?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know what the general purpose would be, but I don't know about this specific case. As far as I know, nothing ugly happened in the town and there was no need to engage such units, unless it was to provide security for buildings, perhaps the municipality building or schools. I know that they provided security for my school in the course of the night in order to prevent anything unfortunate for happening. But as far as I know, there were no particular excessive events, no particular excesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Beforehand you mentioned that there were on a rotation principle some military persons protecting Trnopolje, and now it would be your testimony that in addition to this there was a intervention platoon formed by police forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if it says "order" here, that must be the case. But this police force has nothing to do with Trnopolje. In Trnopolje, for perhaps, I don't know, ten days or maybe more, when members of the Territorial Defence went to the battlefield, the military police was present there, not the civilian police. This relates to the formation of civilian police intervention platoon, not to a military one. This was a group of about ten policemen and they protected the people for a certain period of time over there, and they imprisoned quite a few Serbs who were stealing other people's property there, not really in the camp, that is to say, in the centre, but in the surroundings. I don't know. The people would take all sorts of things from the battlefield. I can't remember what his name was. Cavic. He would take bicycles away. He would take bicycles from people who came to provide their relatives with food. Because every day in Trnopolje at 12.00 a train from Prijedor would arrive and transport friends, relatives of people who had decided to remain in Trnopolje. They would bring them coffee, sugar, things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you then turn to the next page, please. Enactment passed on the 23rd of June, 1992. A little bit more downwards, please, that we can read number 11. "Conclusion to reject the request submitted by Muharem Dauti to return to Stari Grad." Do you recall this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea what this is about. Stari Grad is part of the town where the majority of the population was Muslim, and I don't know what this is about. Perhaps someone seized his property, that is to say, his house. This happened often later on. But at the time it didn't happen very much. But although some people from a town and from around the town decided to come to Trnopolje and to check to see if it was possible for them to go abroad, and perhaps they gave some people their flats or other forms of property. Maybe this person decided not to leave and then decided to request that he be permitted to return to Stari Grad, to his property in Stari Grad. But I don't know what this is about, not exactly. Well, there. I've tried to assist you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would the conclusion be correct that for a Muslim it was necessary to request from the Crisis Staff a decision to return to Stari Grad, as we all know, a destroyed part of the town, most inhabitants Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think that such a request -- that it would be necessary to make such request, and I really don't know. It might appear as if I'm talking off the top of my head, but I don't believe that such decisions were taken by the Crisis Staff. But the members of the executive board were there; that's true. But I really don't know what this is about. It would be reasonable to expect that since you have all these conclusions listed here, there should be conclusions in which someone is being allowed to do this, either here or somewhere else. I can't see any such example here, so I really don't know what it is about. I can't assist you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the moment we're just trying to find out what the Official Gazette of Prijedor is reflecting. Coming now to another enactment of the Crisis Staff passed 22nd June, 1992. Conclusion number 3, "On responsibility for collecting refugees from Cela, Donja Puharska, and Trnopolje." Why this collecting refugees from inter alia Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know which refugees are concerned because there were refugees in Cela, Puharska, and Trnopolje, but these were Serbian refugees who had come from Zenica, Visoko, Donji Vakuf, or rather from the western side, from Bihac, Krupa, Cazin, from Kladusa, et cetera. So perhaps that is what is concerned. But responsibility for collecting refugees from Cela, Donji Puharska, and Trnopolje, I don't know. These other refugees didn't go anywhere. But there weren't any such refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's, please, turn to the next page. Just to give you a possibility. For example, enactment passed the 2nd of July, 1992, "Conclusion coordinating the wartime disposition of the military and police." Why was it for the Crisis Staff to coordinate the wartime disposition of the military and police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. The Secretary for All National Defence, that is, the head of the secretariat, Slavko Budimir, should know the answer to that, because not all people who had different duties to perform could be in the police and the military at one and the same time because this is that time when there was a lot of fighting not in the town and around it but further away. And if a large number of people went with those brigades to the front, then I guess it will be impossible to maintain peace and order in the town, to avoid -- to prevent that from happening, I suppose that there was either request from either the police or the army because the army and is made of people who are citizens, that is, clerks and other people. The army are not soldiers who are getting pay for that. They're ordinary people who have their combat assignment in wartimes. So to prevent that they all go to join some military units, this was to assign them to some police units in order to look after the safety in the town. I suppose that is what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's turn to conclusion number 5, "Recognising -- conclusion recognising time served in the Serbian Territorial Defence and the police as time spent in military training." How was it possible that the Crisis Staff of Prijedor decided or concluded on this issue?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. But once again, I can make assumptions. Again, this has to do with part of people who are within the Crisis Staff, and this has to do with the staff, or rather, the Secretariat for People's Defence. I know that there was a decision to that effect and that in every town, that is, in every secretariat there is an army unit which -- and then they know where it is, what it does. But this is not that one does not have to serve the army by being in the barracks or units. That was not the case then. And now they are preparing a law which will allow people to do their military service at home or doing some public service, community service, or something. But at that time everybody who was under military obligation had a combat assignment in wartime and in peacetime, and this decision recognises in times of the -- in times spent in military training. I suppose it was for that time and that is what these people have in their army cards, in their army booklets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, as to the fact that this is very close to your previous occupation, do you recall this concrete conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: What we've just been talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember this particular conclusion, but I know that it was enforced and that it was recorded in the army booklets of the soldiers, that if people had spent some time at a military exercise, at a military drill, then again this does not mean that they've lost their jobs. No, they were -- they are attending their military exercises and that is a kind of a paid leave. They do not lose their jobs and they don't use any of their years of their time in the regular service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To number 7, "Conclusion concerning the recruitment of persons born in 1974." What has the Crisis Staff of Prijedor to do with the recruitment of persons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Once again, I must start by replying in the same way. This has to do with the Secretary for All National Defence, which was part of the Crisis Staff at the time. These are children -- or rather, young men who were born in 1974 and were to do their military service. And since there is the same Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- or rather, I do not know whether it had already become Republika Srpska by the time and they were its nationals, that is, young men of that age are by law bound to serve the army. Hence, we have this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Number 8, "The conclusion concerning the formation of a committee to receive captured goods." What does that mean "captured goods"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I assume what it could be about. If, for instance, there was a convoy of food or something or some other necessities or if during the combat the owners in some enterprises or somewhere in some companies left something behind, that then that was stolen, if I may put it in those terms, then I suppose the commission took it over officially. As far as I can remember, such things existed and were sent to the Velepromet warehouse and a track record was kept of them. But what kind of records were kept, I do not know. Who handed it over, who took it over, I do not know. But I know that such things were taken to this large commercial enterprise because they had a large warehouse and they kept record of this. Now, where did all these things end up, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, do you recall whether or whether or not you attended this meeting of the Crisis Staff in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't. I don't think so. I don't remember being at any of them. I don't know whether it had already been renamed as the War Presidency. I don't know. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... the 14th of July, 1992 when it was renamed War Presidency? Wasn't it correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the date. I don't know exactly what was the date. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let us go a little bit back on the same page, a little bit higher to the top, please. Conclusion number 4, "Prohibiting the individual releases of persons from Trnopolje, Omarska, and Keraterm." Could you please explain why it was necessary to have a conclusion prohibiting individual releases of persons from Trnopolje, Omarska, and Keraterm, and based on which power could the Crisis Staff come to this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what this is about, and especially with regard to Trnopolje because anyone could go, could leave. For instance, when the train -- everybody could board that train on it way back and leave. I'm not talking about going back to Kozarac, because it wasn't safe there, but perhaps there were some -- perhaps somebody interceded on somebody's behalf or from some institutions outside Prijedor and perhaps some people from Omarska or Keraterm left. But I don't know. I've never been to Keraterm or Omarska, never. I've never crossed the threshold of either. So that as far as I know, in Omarska it was some kind of an investigating prison or centre or whatever. I know that people were interrogated there and those who were not held responsible were let -- were allowed to go, and some of them came to Trnopolje and we fed them there because they had lost some weight, but nobody was ill or anything. But I never talked with those people, and I think a day later after they had had a bath and a decent meal, they just left. They went home or relatives came to fetch them or perhaps they boarded the train and left, so that these individual releases, I know nothing about it. I don't know what kind of a decision was that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... we were just discussing this question. You received, as it was your testimony, inmates of Omarska coming to Trnopolje. Why weren't they released when the interrogation was finalised? Why were they brought to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that I don't know. Believe me. But when they came to Trnopolje it was the same as if they'd been -- become free, because there were no prison rules or rules of conduct or orders. I don't know. Perhaps people did not get proper food up there. Perhaps nobody looked after them properly. I know that a number of them hadn't had their hair cut for quite some time and they had beards and whatnot, so they were allowed to have baths and then their relations came and took them to freedom. But otherwise, I never stopped them from leaving and it wasn't prohibited to leave. I mean, that was not my duty. It wasn't up to me to decide whether somebody could leave or if somebody couldn't leave. My job was to see that those people there were safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you yourself decide spontaneously to release the one or other person on request?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not to -- not freedom. I wouldn't perhaps use that word. But I remember that there were even some military who came to get their relatives from Trnopolje to Banja Luka or Prijedor -- or somewhere -- to Zenica or somewhere else, because they wanted to be together, not because they had been incarcerated there. And I insisted on it being said, and I am saying it in the very best of faith - and I really do not think -- deep in my heart I do not think it was like Omarska or -- that is, I don't think it was anything like a prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you would say Omarska was a prison?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, I know that officially it was an investigation centre. Now, what, how -- like everybody else on television, I heard, and from those who were there that -- part of the Muslim people and those who, I mean, guarded there, the police and all the others, that there were some problems there. But believe me, personally I know nothing about that because I never put my foot there, in any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Didn't you speak with previous inmates of Omarska or Keraterm about the conditions they were subjected to when detained in Omarska and Keraterm, when they came later to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: No. With those from Keraterm, I never talked with them nor did they ever come from Keraterm -- at least, I don't remember that.
