And those over there in Omarska, from what I remember that conversation, there were people -- I think they had some three groups, A, B, and C, those who had attacked Prijedor or participated in this and then group C who had nothing to do with anything and they were allowed to come over here and go home, except that once at some point a group of women arrived. I don't remember how many. I think there were about 30, perhaps 31 or 32, who came from Omarska. I don't know how long they were kept. I know some of them by sight, but I don't really remember their names because they were much younger than I. And this Jadranka Cigelg was with them, who then later on wrote all sorts of things. Whether it's all like what she wrote or perhaps her friends, I don't know. One should talk with people who were there, but I never talked with them and I didn't talk with those either. But I did my best when they arrived to provide them with decent documentation, to get warm water, to be able to have a bath, a change of clothes, and then people from town came and took them away. And what happened after that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Those 30 to 32 women, they arrived from Omarska; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... any special rooms for the women in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, no special rooms. I think there was one house or perhaps two adjacent, and those neighbours there, those people there, we asked them to prepare some hot water from wells or from pumps. I mean, Muslim women who lived there. Some were there in the neighbourhood and they all prepared that and they had their baths and washed themselves. Whether they spent one night or one evening there, I can't remember exactly. And then they left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Previously you talked about alleged rapes in Trnopolje. Once again, I have to recall that it's your right to remain silent on this issue if you feel that a true answer could tend to a kind of self-incrimination. Have you ever been seen or such a rape have you, to come to the point, participated in such a rape?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never saw that. I never participated in it. I think there was this one case one night and then in the morning when I arrived there with representatives of the Red Cross we came together as every day to organise the meals and everything else. Then we heard that that had happened, and the police came and took them over and then interrogated them, who had done it, why had he done it, and then the doctors examined them and they returned, and after that I didn't interfere. I didn't really talk with those women what had happened and how it had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Where did you actually live during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I was living at home, in Prijedor. Every day before nightfall I would go back home, because -- I mean, guards stayed there to look after people there. I never spent a night in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to remove his fingers from his mouth.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: And I suppose some of the people lived in the neighbourhood and some of them returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The interpreter booths ask that could you please kindly withdraw your fingers from your lips; otherwise, it's difficult for them to understand.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Isn't it true, Mr. Kuruzovic, that there was a private house close to Trnopolje centre you had for your own purposes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't call it that. By and large the houses all around were inhabited. And there was one house where at times we had lunch together. Those from the Red Cross or I would be with them and there were also two guys who were often with me, who looked after me, protected me. But we'd only have a meal there. I was often among the people in the school or outside in the camp because I was there to organise, to lend a hand, to prepare food, to see that the bread was brought, to look after children. And whenever there would be a problem, they'd call me because they knew that I would intercede with the Red Cross and to do something about that, about whatever had happened to make the situation tolerable as possible because it was summertime and it was hot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We'll come back to this when we have a look on the map and a video later on. You told us about people arriving. Would it be true that they arrived in buses from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this group that I talked about, yes, they arrived by bus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what would be your overall assessment how many people left Trnopolje in the direction of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. 2.000 maybe, 3.000. I don't know. I never paid any particular attention, nor did we count them or take down their names. They left. Nor the Red Cross didn't count them, nor those who were with the security, but they were issued certificates that they'd been there and they left, except when there was the UNHCR, they took them away. So I suppose they made some lists, but then they left with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who issued these certificates and why was it necessary to have a certificate to leave?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, it wasn't a certificate allowing one to leave. It's a certificate to show that that person, a man, a woman, the whole family, that they were there, in Trnopolje. That was a kind of certificate. Because that is what the International Red Cross and the UNHCR requested of us to do, and the members of the Red Cross from Prijedor who were there day in, day out, they issued those certificates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How many of them left voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, an overwhelming majority left because they wanted to go to get out of the region which was Republika Srpska. They wanted to join their own people. Some didn't leave of their own volition because they wanted to but because their relations, their friends, their neighbours had gone, that is, those who lived next to them. So those had left and these perhaps didn't want to but then they left -- they followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did they leave on buses of Autotransport Prijedor? Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, buses of the Autotransport came to Trnopolje and took them away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You already mentioned this heinous crime committed at Mount Vlasic. Could you please testify in context about what you learned at that time and what you know now about that what happened finally resulting in the deaths of about 228 persons at Mount Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that I learned about it two or three days later. I don't remember exactly. And as I was there as a member of the brigade of the army and the Commander Arsic even asked me to write a report about what had happened. That day when I learnt about that, I wrote it, but I had no idea that it had happened or anything like it, but it seems that a group of those escorts from the police had got together and it seems that they had decided amongst themselves to do something as horrific as that. Later on I heard that they singled out a group of men, took money and jewellery and I don't know what else from everybody, from men and women. I don't know whether it is true or not because I have no information about that. But I know that the majority of those people were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know names of these persons being personally responsible for these heinous crimes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't so help me. Once last year at about this time in Banja Luka, when I was there making my statement, I was asked about that, but you shouldn't be surprised that I do not know that. At that time I was already 50, and I had nothing to do for the past ten years or so with those who are 20 or 25 years old, so I don't know them. But I remember that those were by and large young men who on various occasions escorted those buses. And every time everything was all right I remember them calling by telephone. And then on that particular occasion something completely different happened, something that is -- that our people does not do. But I guess it was because of some material gain that it was done. That is not a trait of our people. I don't know those names. I think that one of them was called Babin. Perhaps I remember it because I know that he was wounded later on in combat, that he's in a wheelchair. Otherwise, who those others were, I don't remember because they are much younger than that I, so that I don't even know their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Mrdja?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Mrdja? I know Dado Mrdja, yes. He was a pupil of mine. But I can't remember whether he was in that group when this incident occurred, related to the escort -- the bus being escorted. But I know him personally. Later I was told that when this happened that they had taken him from Prijedor and that that was one of the reasons for which he had been brought to The Hague, but that's something I found out later. Like many other people, I did not remember -- I did not like to recall these events, the wartime events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to show the last pages of document S250, please. It's very close to the end already. It's just -- The purpose, do you recall that you were present when one of these enactments were passed in July 1992? For example, number 14, a "Decision to rename the Crisis Staff the War Presidency"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I was there. I know that it was renamed. Perhaps I was present, but I can't be sure. As I said, since I no longer had the duties of commander, I can't remember whether I was present at that meeting. Since I was no longer the commander, I no longer had the duty of attending the sessions of the Crisis Staff or of the working president -- of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But from time to time, you attended; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But, in fact, the Crisis Staff was then renamed War Presidency; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's a well-known fact. But I don't know what the date was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... So then finally, to conclude before the break, a decision, "All the enactments are hereby confirmed," and then president of the municipal assembly, Dr. Milomir Stakic. Did you participate in this meeting of the municipal assembly when all these enactments were confirmed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I was -- I had a mandate as a deputy for the assembly. But whether that happened during that period, I can't remember. If that's the case, then the official assembly confirmed this, a decision was taken, and the president of the assembly had the duty of signing the assembly decision. There are a lot of dates, so I can't remember exactly. Believe me, I can't even remember when I was a deputy, whether it was in 1992 or 1993 or 1994. I really can't remember. I think it was later on, but I don't know. When I was a deputy in the assembly, perhaps it was in 1993 or 1994, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The trial stays adjourned until ten minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Madam Registrar, for the transcript, the video that is prepared has Exhibit number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: J22, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could the video please be started. And Mr. Kuruzovic, whenever you want to comment on what you're seeing on the screen, the usher has provided it in a way that the video is shown -- please say "stop" when you want to comment on this, what you can see on the screen. Please start the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We had asked to be taken to a second camp --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can stop right here. On the other side, where you can see these people, there is a yard. It's the yard of the centre in Trnopolje. And on this side of the fence, towards us, there is the warehouse of the agricultural association. The fence -- the wire fence you can see here is about 8 metres long. I don't know exactly. You've got this barbed wire and this mesh wire, but at no other location can you come across -- could you come across a wire fence, apart from the school's fence behind which there was a hedge, et cetera. But this young man here -- later on I heard that he had medical problems, so he didn't have this appearance because he had been starved by someone but simply because he was that kind of a man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: THE SPEAKER: And which has also been at the centre of allegations of atrocities. Conditions at this camp were appalling. In 100-degree heat, hundreds of men were forced to eat and sleep outside in a field, behind barbed wire. Their meagre rations consist of a small hunk of bread and a bowl of soup every day. Here, too, they said they had been rounded up, whole villages emptied of their men, and they were afraid. Can you tell me anything about the conditions that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was some other fence, the sequence before this one. That's the one, here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: THE SPEAKER: They said they had been rounded up, whole villages emptied of their men, and they were afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That one there. That wasn't the fence in Trnopolje. That one had a different shape. I don't know where this one was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you please rewind. Stop. Continue a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: THE SPEAKER: And they were afraid. Can you tell me anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop. This is in Trnopolje; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. If I viewed this a little longer, maybe I could say. I can remember this film. I saw it on television. It was on television. But I would like to repeat: Behind them, there were no fences of any kind. There was an asphalt road. And to the right there was a low fence, perhaps between 80 centimetres and a metre high from the yard of the centre and then from the yard of the school, so there were no fences really. Or it would be better to say that it didn't resemble a prison of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: THE SPEAKER: I am not sure that I am allowed about that. Can you understand me? SPEAKER 1: Are people here being beaten? THE SPEAKER: Here? Here, no. Here? I rather wouldn't talk about that. I'm not sure. SPEAKER 1: Can you tell us anything about the conditions that you were being kept in and the treatment of the people you were with? THE SPEAKER: Well, that was hard time, hard to say. SPEAKER 1: We heard -- we heard stories of people being beaten and people disappearing. Did that happen? THE SPEAKER: Well, I can't say much about that. THE SPEAKER: We just came here. SPEAKER 1: From another camp. THE SPEAKER: From another camp. And we didn't know the condition here. We accept a little more better, like -- SPEAKER 1: What was it like before? THE SPEAKER: It was terrible. SPEAKER 1: One of the prisoners asked us to check on him in several days time to see that he hadn't been punished for speaking to us. And away from the camera there were allegations of routine beatings and executions. Several prisoners told us of retaliatory killings. One instance in which they claimed 150 of their fellow prisoners had been killed following the death of 10 Serbian soldiers in a Muslim village. We were told people had been beaten to death and we were asked to smuggle a film out of the camp. The pictures show severe injuries, apparently as a result of beatings. In the make-shift medical centre there were cases of scabies, malnutrition, and diarrhoea. Local doctors said they were chronically short of medicine and drugs. Among them was a Muslim doctor. We asked him whether there had been any cases of beatings. On one side of the camp were refugees who were here simply because they have nowhere else to go. Their homes having been destroyed. They have been told they can go as soon as they have a guarantee of a home outside Serb-controlled Bosnia. In Banja Luka, prisoners' wives have been queuing for days for news of their men and to register as refugees because they, too, have nowhere to go. On the roads to Banja Luka, Muslim villages lie empty and deserted, homes destroyed. If there is eventually freedom for the men in the detention centres, it's not likely to be in Serb-controlled Bosnia. Ian Williams, ITN, Northern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you want to comment on this video clip?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can see that there are people here, and to the extent that I understand English, you could see that some of them had come from other places and that in those other places they had been physically beaten. I know that in Trnopolje this was never done, and this Pilovac Amata [phoen], this young doctor, I think there was another doctor whose name was Pasic with him and there were two nurses and a medical orderly, a medical orderly without an arm also came very often and another doctor from the town. So to the extent that this was possible, good care was taken of the health of those people. But how some people ended up in Trnopolje, these are questions that I cannot answer directly because I didn't question anyone in Trnopolje and there were never investigations of any kind, no one was ever examined. These people were there as a result of the problems caused by the fighting. They came there to take shelter. But we did speak about this matter before the break. We said that there was a group of people who came there. There were people who didn't do anything bad. They'd come to Trnopolje from Omarska. But as you can see, a large number of them were naked above the waist not because they were forced not to wear anything above the waist but it was hot. It was very sunny weather. And I'm not saying this to mock anyone. This was the truth. It was easier for people when they took some of their clothes off. It's not as if I wanted to say something ugly here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there place enough for all of them to sleep inside the building?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: No, there wasn't enough room in the building. I apologise. Perhaps I started too soon. No, there wasn't enough room in the school. We made an effort for women and children and the elderly to go there, but the men -- well, we didn't force anyone to stay outside. In the beginning the people used their freight vehicles, the tarpaulins of those vehicles, the tractors, cars, et cetera, and then they put blankets under them. The weather was good. It was summer weather. And then I asked the director Diko Mrakovica, a friend from school, and then there was an assistant there too. I can't remember his name. I think his name was Stijepic. They gave us parts of nets that were used for placing concrete for the foundations of houses. These were sort of meshes. We brought that over and then people from the UNHCR brought a lot of nylon, blue nylon, and then people made tents of a certain kind and closed it on two sides, and the third side was free, it was open, and then they would put blankets down on the ground. But most people had some form of shelter. They were covered. They weren't out in the open. Some of those young -- some of those children, the small children, found accommodation in the houses of those Muslims who were living there in their houses, and that's because the children were young and there were some elderly people there. That was right next to the school. There were quite a few houses there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown Exhibit number 321-2. Starting with the school building, could you please tell us what are these other buildings.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Here -- the houses here surrounding this area are private houses. Here you have the club and then the local commune building, the clinic and the post office. Here behind, that's an old club, an old centre. There's a big hall there and there is one room. And here you have the agricultural association. On this side of the road there's a standard metal fence, and there was a small fence, wire fence here. Here we have the road, and this is the fence that was shown in the clip a minute ago. This has been knocked down. You don't have a fence that joins up with the other fence. There's only something here. Here you have the fence that wasn't joined up. Across the road you have a house that had a telephone. I can't remember now, but I think that this house belonged to a man who worked in the school, at the reception, and the Red Cross was there on a daily basis and all services that had to do with writing out certificates and that had to do with telephone conversations with some of their relatives took place here. I spent most of my time here with them, every day. I tried to deal with various problems. I heard about whether there were any problems here in the school. And here on this side of the school there was a water pump. It was possible to get water from there, and there was water inside, the school. Here in front, in front of the clinic there was a shop which was open for a long time and it was possible to buy food there. It was possible to get food there. Here in front of the school there was some kind of a fence, about a metre high, a standard fence, and behind it there was a hedge and there was a small wooden fence here and here too, a small wooden fence here too. And here on the other side in front of the school there was a school fence and there's a school fence here too. And on this side here you had one kitchen and here you had another kitchen where food was prepared, but I think that in one of these houses here there were people, local people who lived in their houses and they would slaughter their cattle and then they would bring food over here. That's how they fed themselves. Here at the back you have a football pitch. This is the road to Prijedor. And then as there was no longer enough room here -- and Your Honour, you asked me about this a while ago. As there was not enough room in the school, they used this area here behind the school and the football pitch and over here on this side in the yard. People put up the wire that we brought and covered it with the nylon provided by the UNHCR and the International Red Cross from Banja Luka and they made tents here and people took shelter there, the people who couldn't find accommodation, who couldn't be accommodated in the school and in this school -- in this club here. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Where would be the house one could call your premises?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they weren't my premises. I spent most of the time here. As there were a lot of people here very often, they were queuing up and so on. And now I can't remember whether it was this house here, because there was another smaller one here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please raise that part. Would it be correct at the right-hand side, the house at the right-hand side, on the top?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. Just a minute. This is the fence in front of the club, the centre. We have the school here. Somewhere around here, that's where the house was, and this is where we would usually eat. The people from the Red Cross would come here and we would eat together. We also received those lunch packets because there was a problem as far as food is concerned in the town, and this is where we would eat together. On several occasions there were a number of families in this house. At the beginning I think there were four families, some women with children, and there was one woman with a child. I think she had two children, two girls. I can't remember. And then later on a large family came to these houses. They all waited there together. They wanted to link up with their families. They wanted to go abroad. And in these other houses there were also a lot of people. They were there as guests in the houses of the hosts because these Muslim citizens were in their houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to present this in part redacted document - because this part is confidential - S12B. And please put it on the ELMO. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I can see that there's something there, but I don't know what it is. Perhaps someone came -- from one of their own, from far away, from Banja Luka, and wanted to take that person away without any problems. And it was necessary if this person left to provide a justification, to show that he was there and that he wasn't taken away for some ugly reasons, for example, because someone had killed him or something like that. Pero Curguz was a representative of the Red Cross. And they probably took this decision that this person - man or woman, I don't know - should leave. And I confirmed that this person had been brought here, had been brought to the Red Cross and had left to avoid ugly consequences of any kind so that it couldn't be said that one didn't know what had happened to the person. So it would be known that someone had taken him away. This is what I assume. I don't know if it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: There's my signature here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the left-hand side is your signature. You recognise this as your signature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what was the purpose to issue this, as it reads, "receipt"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: This one here and all the other receipts, I said that they were all issued so that one could be sure that the people were there and so that no one could take them away if they did not desire this. I don't know what this is about, but I assume -- I can see what it says here. It says "discharged on the basis of the decision," and then what does it say? "Leaving the Autonomous Region of Krajina," and then there's a certain number. Someone must have issued this decision on leaving the Autonomous Region of Krajina from Banja Luka. I don't know who it was. I don't know who came. They wanted to take that person away. And I never allowed anyone to leave Trnopolje just like that. But if someone wanted to do so, he could do so but it was necessary to inform the Red Cross. Without such an official record, these are things that would not be known. One would not know why he had been taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Usher, this can be brought back to the Registry. Mr. Kuruzovic, you know Mr. Slavko Puhalic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was in Trnopolje very often. And as far as I know, he's a member of the military police. He helped the people from the Red Cross and he helped me when Serbs living in the surrounding villages, the surrounding houses, when they came and took things from houses. There were even situations when the people who were further away from Trnopolje - I think it's Suvi Brod - I don't know exactly. It's in the direction of Kozarac. Well, they would seize their property. They would loot. They would engage in looting. They would take their stove, firewood, corn, et cetera. I don't know when these people came to see me and asked me to help them and they said that people from Petrov Gaj would come and take their things. So sometimes I would send Slavko to control this, to check this, and then to return and then they would bring these things and very often I sent the military police and had Serbs imprisoned. There was a certain Cavic who caused problems, who stole bicycles, did all sorts of things. Naturally, there were people among my people who were not respectful, who were not worthy of respect, and they took advantage of this opportunity to loot and to steal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be correct, then that, Slavko Puhalic is also known as Ture Mesar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: I've never heard that that was his nickname Ture Mesar? Never heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who was your deputy as commander of the Trnopolje open reception centre?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: To begin with, I've already told you. I wasn't the commander. I was some kind of an organiser, an intermediary between the police, the Red Cross, the municipal authorities. So I had to have somebody whose job it would be to look after that place. And secondly, I didn't have any deputy. Whatever I need by way of food or intervention of the police or anything, I would ask for that through the commander of the Red Cross or the executive board, or if we needed buses, if people had expressed the wish to go, then again I'd do that. I'd contact Mr. Mico Kovacevic and send buses and the buses would come and that was that. Unless, perhaps, he - I'm not quite sure - but as our people say, put on airs, and perhaps introduce himself as a kind of a deputy. But I didn't have a deputy in that sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Didn't you claim that your deputy was the commander of the security unit on duty, page 72 of your statement last year?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: No. Perhaps you didn't understand me correctly. The army -- or rather, those who guarded those people, who provided security, they were under the command of their unit's commander. For instance, there were several battalions in that one brigade, and from one battalion say a unit comes a platoon strong, so 20, 30 men, and they then guard the whole street and they have their commander who is the commander based on military rules. I would just go there to see that they are deployed properly, to take over the shift. But that was the man who commanded them. I merely organised things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When asked in March last year, page 72, you were asked, "Who was your deputy if you're not there? Who would take care of any problems which might arise in the reception centre?" Your answer was at that time, "It would always be the one who is the commander of the security unit, of the unit for the security."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes. The soldiers who came, and their commander, he was responsible for the safety of those people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then you continued, "Well, nobody officially actually replaced me while I was not there, but it usually happened that a bit later than myself Slavko Puhalic would stay. But as much as I know, he never spent overnight either. So practically officially the deputies were the commanders of the units." Would you stick to your testimony at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Slavko Puhalic never did anything like that. I don't know what was the context in which I said it, but officially he had no duty there except as far as I know that he was a member of the military police and at times would turn up there. But that's all. But I was never there at night. Whether Slavko came at night, I do not know that. I suppose he was not, but perhaps he did. And if something happened there at that time, then it should be the commander of the unit who was guarding the place at the time who should know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You were appointed to you duty - let's call it this way - and for which period of time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it just happens so. I told you who called me. That was the late Simo and the late Dr. Kovacevic. And I told you already that I was angry. Why had they decided I should go there? And I went there to see if that was true, what was being said, that those people were getting there, and I went there, and I saw it and I helped those people to be accommodated there and that is how it set off, spontaneously, if that's the word. Because I am that kind of man. By nature I am very sentimental, I am very sensitive, and it was difficult for me to see people, as our people would say, how day after day after day it went on and nobody said how long was it supposed to last. And when I was there together with all those people inside, I could see that all these promises, that someday people would be united together, families be joined, and they would go abroad, get their families there, and then -- or either there and leave abroad together or meet other members of their family abroad. Then I just talked to those people inside, that it had to be disbanded, that it was really not all right to go on because the autumn was coming, there would be problems with food and safety and then -- and fuel, and then the centre simply ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... discuss the problems emanating from this centre in the framework of the Crisis Staff or with other members of the Crisis Staff or bilaterally with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that any one of them was unaware of its existence or of its operation. I think that once Dr. Stakic helped because Dr. Mico -- I mean, the late Dr. Mico to ensure the transportation. I don't know how many. They asked for two buses or perhaps three buses for people; otherwise, any other subject I don't know. But I don't think that there was anyone who was not aware of the existence, of its existence. But then one -- that's not really the right way, the correct way to speak about that. But the late Professor Koljevic - and I know that - frequently called Simo Drljaca, the deceased, and said to look after all those people properly so that no -- there shouldn't be any killing or anything. Whether it was with his authorisation or somebody else's, with documents in writing almost daily, news agencies came, BBC, Reuters, or even journalists from Yugoslavia, from Novi Sad and so forth. Mr. Mazowiecki was there, and also Mr. Kouchner. Also later I heard on television how they had objected to the living conditions there, but I didn't hear -- at least, none of them told me anything. But I am not saying that it was easy, because it wasn't. But it wasn't all that unbearable because we tried to help people to survive and the proof of that is in the fact that nobody died there, there were no outbreaks of epidemics, children were born there, and I even helped them to roast lambs on Bajram, because that's their custom. I've forgotten to say that, but now I'm saying it because I had nothing against that, of course. One had to respect it. That was their religion and those others who created problems, that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned just a minute before that once Dr. Stakic helped to ensure the transportation. Could you please tell us, what did you mean by this helping to ensure the transportation? Of whom and transportation from where to where?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in that regard, I always provided it whenever people asked, and then one goes through Travnik to Central Bosnia, that is, through the area where the majority of the population are Muslims. And I saw this through Mr. Mico Kovacevic because he's the president of the executive board and then he'd call Autotransport and the manager there would provide the buses because also the fuel had to be provided for those buses, for the departure, and I think that the late Dr. Mico Kovacevic wasn't there and that Mr. Stakic did it. When was that exactly? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned during your testimony today that sometimes it happened that military personnel asked for the release of relatives or other persons. Who would have the final say on the release requested? Would it be you, the police, or the military?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, come on. It was the Red Cross who decided. But those were people who came, who had their godfathers, friends, relatives. But as a rule, it was the other way around: Serbs and some military personnel brought some of their relatives or neighbours, their best men, and asked us to be -- to receive them in Trnopolje because they wanted to leave Prijedor and establish communication with their families. And I would get angry at times because I was afraid that something would happen to those people and nobody would be wise to that. I didn't think that someday they would come, that I would be sitting there and answer those problems. But those are the problems that occurred in the life of those people who lived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... if a witness would testify that when approaching Trnopolje he was directed to you and asked you in person whether he could leave together with relatives and you granted and said, "No problem, you can leave with your relatives"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, possibly there were such instances when I said that yes, that person could go, and that they should be issued with those certificates to show that they'd been there, and that they then left. I don't see why should there be any problem. Why couldn't they leave? As I've said, I would have been the happiest if there were much fewer of them there or if nobody was there because there was always this danger hanging there that one of those irresponsible people or those who, although they are Serbs, but still are nevertheless brigands at heart and looters and then problems arise and it's difficult to steer clear of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes your today's testimony. It will be only a short period of time we will continue to the Judges, with the line of Judges' questions tomorrow morning. And then only that the parties know as to the fact that Mr. Kuruzovic appeared on the list of the requested Defence witnesses. It would be for the first time to put questions to the witness for the Defence and then later for the Prosecution. The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00, in this same courtroom, number I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: at 4.36 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 27th day of March, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
